stem: Child with mass in the abdomen in the left flank Ultrasound: Confirmed a mass with internal calcification What is the Most Appropriate Next test to reach the diagnosis (The Examiner Confirmed The Stem Was Exactly Like This)
highlight_terms_source: mass in the abdomen in the left flank
why_right: A child with a flank mass showing internal calcification on ultrasound suggests neuroblastoma (calcification is typical) over Wilms tumor. The lead-in asks for the most appropriate NEXT test: after ultrasound, the next step is cross-sectional imaging, and CT defines the organ of origin, extent, vascular encasement and nodes before any tissue sampling. This recall's key is CT as the next step, with biopsy coming afterwards for the definitive diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI is an acceptable alternative cross-sectional study (no radiation, good for spinal canal extension), but CT is the classic exam answer for the next imaging step and shows calcification best.
C. Biopsy gives the definitive diagnosis but is done after CT has mapped the mass and planned the approach. It is the answer when the word 'next' is absent and the question asks for the test that confirms the diagnosis (see the paired recall).
key_concept:
Pediatric abdominal mass ladder: US first, then CT (or MRI), then biopsy for tissue diagnosis.
  • 'Next test' after US: CT
  • 'Confirm / reach the diagnosis' without 'next': biopsy
  • Calcification + crosses midline + ill child: neuroblastoma
  • No calcification, intrarenal, well child, does not cross midline: Wilms
  • Neuroblastoma extras: urine catecholamines (VMA/HVA), bone marrow, MIBG
exam_pearl: Read the lead-in: 'next' test = CT; 'confirm the diagnosis' = biopsy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Numbered 512; compiler notes the examiner confirmed this stem exactly. Related variants 513 to 516 follow as separate numbers.

stem: A 3 year old child comes with a large mass on his flank side that was found incidentally. The mass is hard, firm, and not mobile. On xray it shows soft tissue mass with internal calcifications. What is the next step in to establish the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: soft tissue mass with internal calcifications
why_right: A 3-year-old with a hard, fixed flank mass and calcifications on X-ray points to neuroblastoma. The lead-in asks for the next step to establish the diagnosis: plain film only shows a soft tissue mass, so the next step is cross-sectional imaging. CT abdomen confirms the organ of origin, extent and calcification and plans the biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI abdomen is a reasonable alternative in some centres, especially for suspected spinal extension, but CT is the standard exam answer for the next imaging step after X-ray or US.
C. Biopsy gives the tissue diagnosis but comes after CT has defined the lesion; it is the answer when the question asks how to confirm the diagnosis rather than the next step.
D. Bone marrow aspiration is part of neuroblastoma staging (marrow spread) once the primary is characterized. It is the first test for suspected leukemia (pallor, bruising, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias), not for an isolated flank mass.
key_concept:
Child + flank mass + calcification: image (CT) before tissue.
  • X-ray or US first finding: then CT abdomen
  • Then biopsy for histology
  • Then staging: bone marrow, MIBG, urine VMA/HVA
  • Bone marrow first: suspected leukemia with cytopenias
exam_pearl: Bone marrow aspiration is staging for neuroblastoma, not the next step for a flank mass.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 512 (x-ray rather than ultrasound; adds bone marrow aspiration option). Compiler wrote an Arabic aside that the imaging was x-ray.

stem: Child with mass in the abdomen in the left flank Ultrasound: Confirmed a mass with internal calcification What is the Most Appropriate test to reach the diagnosis (The Word "Next" Not Present , I Am SURE 100%)
highlight_terms_source: mass in the abdomen in the left flank
why_right: Same child with a left flank mass with internal calcification on ultrasound, but here the lead-in asks for the most appropriate test to reach the diagnosis with no word 'next'. A malignant pediatric abdominal mass (neuroblastoma vs Wilms) is diagnosed definitively only by histology, so referral for biopsy is the test that establishes the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI characterizes and stages the mass but cannot give a histological diagnosis; it is an alternative to CT as the next imaging step.
B. CT is the right answer when the question asks for the NEXT test after ultrasound (the paired recall). It describes the mass but does not prove what it is.
key_concept:
Lead-in decides the answer for the same stem.
  • 'Most appropriate NEXT test': CT
  • 'Test to reach / confirm the diagnosis': biopsy
  • Option combining CT and biopsy: choose it when 'next' is absent
exam_pearl: Imaging suggests, histology diagnoses: drop the word 'next' and the answer becomes biopsy.

stem: Child with mass in the abdomen in the left flank Ultrasound: Confirmed a mass with internal calcification What is the Most Appropriate test to reach the diagnosis (The Word "Next" Not Present , I Am SURE 100%)
OptB: CT & Biopsy (Together In Same Option , 100% Sure)
highlight_terms_source: mass in the abdomen in the left flank
why_right: For a flank mass with internal calcification in a child, reaching the diagnosis needs both steps: CT to define the organ of origin, extent and spread, and biopsy for the histological diagnosis (neuroblastoma vs Wilms vs other). With no 'next' in the lead-in, the option that combines CT and biopsy covers the complete diagnostic work-up.
why_wrong_block: A. MRI alone is only an imaging alternative to CT; it stages the mass but gives no tissue diagnosis, so it cannot by itself reach the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Pediatric solid abdominal mass work-up: US, then CT (or MRI), then biopsy.
  • 'Next test': CT
  • 'Confirm diagnosis': biopsy
  • 'CT and biopsy' together offered: pick it
exam_pearl: When CT and biopsy appear in one option, it beats any single imaging test for 'reaching the diagnosis'.

stem: A child with a 2 cm skin colored painless abdominal mass, otherwise normal. What is the Diagnostic test ? (Written Exactly Like This) Calcifications Not Mentioned
highlight_terms_source: 2 cm skin colored painless abdominal mass
why_right: This recall's key is abdominal CT as the diagnostic test for a 2 cm painless abdominal mass in an otherwise normal child. The source's reasoning treats CT as the cross-sectional test that defines the origin, depth and nature of an abdominal mass before any tissue sampling, in line with the CT-first pattern of the related abdominal mass recalls.
why_wrong_block:
B. Biopsy is not the first diagnostic test for a small painless mass in a well child; it follows imaging and is the answer when the question asks how to confirm a suspected malignancy.
C. Ultrasound is the usual first-line, radiation-free study for a superficial or abdominal mass in a child; it is the answer when the question asks for the initial test.
D. MRI is an alternative cross-sectional study, used when radiation should be avoided or soft tissue detail is needed, but it was not the recalled key.
key_concept:
Child with abdominal mass: match the test to the lead-in.
  • Initial / first test: ultrasound
  • Diagnostic cross-sectional test (this recall's key): CT
  • Confirm tissue diagnosis: biopsy
  • MRI: radiation-sparing alternative to CT
exam_pearl: 'Initial' test for a pediatric mass is usually ultrasound; this recall keys CT for 'diagnostic test'.

stem: 3 years old came with huge palpable abdominal mass. How to CONFIRM the Diagnosis?
why_right: A 3-year-old with a huge palpable abdominal mass raises concern for a solid malignancy such as Wilms tumor or neuroblastoma. The lead-in asks how to CONFIRM the diagnosis, and only histology confirms the nature of a tumor, so biopsy is the answer.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT defines the organ of origin, extent and spread and is the right answer for the next imaging step, but it cannot prove the histology.
B. Ultrasound is the initial test to confirm that a mass exists and whether it is solid or cystic; it is right for 'first' or 'initial' investigation, not for confirming the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Lead-in verbs for a pediatric abdominal mass:
  • Initial test: ultrasound
  • Next / best imaging: CT (or MRI)
  • Confirm the diagnosis: biopsy (histology)
exam_pearl: 'Confirm' means tissue: imaging never confirms a tumor's type.

stem: A Child Presents With fever and irritability and red warm Painful Tender swelling in the lower part of the left leg. There is no pus or abscess but the area is Enlarging. All vitals are stable and there are no Other systemic manifestations
why_right: A red, warm, tender, enlarging swelling of the leg with no pus or abscess is non-purulent cellulitis, and the child has fever and irritability, meaning systemic features. Cellulitis with systemic signs warrants IV antibiotics rather than oral outpatient therapy, and an enlarging lesion in a febrile child needs surgical review to exclude a deep collection or necrotizing infection early. Stable vitals do not change this; they only mean ICU care is not needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral flucloxacillin is right for mild, localized cellulitis without fever; topical antibiotics have no role for cellulitis (they are for superficial impetigo). Here fever and an enlarging lesion call for IV therapy.
B. Flucloxacillin with outpatient follow up fits a mild cellulitis in a well, afebrile child. This child is febrile, irritable and the area is spreading, so outpatient management is inadequate.
key_concept:
Cellulitis severity decides the route.
  • Mild, no systemic signs: oral anti-staphylococcal antibiotic, follow up
  • Fever or systemic signs, or spreading: admit, IV antibiotics
  • Abscess or fluctuation: drainage (surgical consult)
  • Pain out of proportion, crepitus, rapid spread, toxicity: urgent surgical debridement
  • No fluctuation = no abscess to drain
exam_pearl: Fever turns cellulitis into an IV antibiotic problem even when vitals are otherwise stable.

stem: 10-year-old child progressive respiratory distress, after severe pneumonia. Given oxygen therapy (no antibiotic usage was mentioned Whatsoever!), with no improvements still hypoxia. Done cardio exam and echo normal, what's the associated or what will you find on his x-ray?
OptA: Haemoptysis and no something else, I forgot what it was.
key_concept:
Refractory hypoxia after pneumonia: decide cardiac vs lung vs airway.
  • Normal echo excludes cardiogenic pulmonary edema
  • ARDS: acute insult within a week, hypoxia not corrected by oxygen, bilateral infiltrates, non-cardiac
  • Bronchopneumonia: patchy bilateral infiltrates with fever and crackles
  • Lobar pneumonia: single lobe consolidation
  • Apical consolidation or cavity: think TB
  • Hyperinflation with wheeze: asthma, bronchiolitis, bronchiolitis obliterans
exam_pearl: Let the stem's clue decide: oxygen-refractory hypoxia with a normal echo fits a non-cardiogenic diffuse pattern, while haemoptysis, apical disease or wheeze each need their own specific clue.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler: 'B/C??' (undecided between B and C).
Other marked answers: Compiler: B/C??
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Macrosomia baby has weak moro reflux what is the next step?
why_right: A "macrosomia baby" is at risk of shoulder dystocia, and a weak Moro reflex (on the affected side) after such a delivery points to brachial plexus injury, usually Erb palsy (C5 to C6). Most cases recover spontaneously, so the initial management is conservative: gentle immobilization of the arm across the body (avoid traction) and supportive care, followed by physiotherapy with passive range of motion. Surgery is reserved for infants with no recovery after a few months.
why_wrong_block:
B. Surgical nerve exploration/repair is considered only if function does not recover after about 3 to 6 months, not as the next step in a newborn.
C. Calcium supplements treat neonatal hypocalcemia (e.g., infant of a diabetic mother), which causes jitteriness or seizures, not a weak one-sided Moro.
D. Dextrose treats neonatal hypoglycemia, common in macrosomic infants of diabetic mothers, but that produces jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy or seizures rather than a focal weak Moro.
key_concept:
Macrosomia + asymmetric/weak Moro = birth trauma (brachial plexus injury or clavicle fracture).
  • Erb palsy (C5 to C6): "waiter's tip" arm, absent Moro on that side, grasp preserved
  • Klumpke palsy (C8 to T1): claw hand, absent grasp
  • Management: immobilization, supportive care, physiotherapy
  • No recovery by about 3 to 6 months: refer for surgery
  • Hypoglycemia/hypocalcemia: global signs (jitteriness, seizures), not a one-arm deficit
exam_pearl: A focal one-sided reflex loss means a local (nerve or bone) injury; global depressed reflexes point to metabolic or CNS causes.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0390).

stem: pregnant 38 weeks uncontrolled DM delivered macrosomic baby by SVD, the child has week moro reflex on the right side, most appropriate management?
OptC: Immobilization of affected arm and support
highlight_terms_source: week moro reflex on the right side
why_right: A macrosomic baby of a mother with uncontrolled diabetes, delivered vaginally, is at risk of shoulder dystocia and brachial plexus (Erb) injury, which explains a weak Moro reflex on one side. Most Erb palsies recover spontaneously, so initial management is conservative: gently immobilize the arm across the body for comfort for the first days, then start passive range of motion physiotherapy to prevent contractures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Surgery (nerve exploration or repair) is reserved for infants without recovery of elbow flexion (biceps) after a few months of conservative care, not for a newborn.
B. IV dextrose treats neonatal hypoglycemia, a real risk in infants of diabetic mothers, but hypoglycemia gives jitteriness, poor feeding or seizures and a symmetric picture, not a one-sided weak Moro.
key_concept:
Asymmetric Moro after a difficult delivery = brachial plexus injury or clavicle fracture.
  • Risk: macrosomia, infant of diabetic mother, shoulder dystocia
  • Erb palsy: C5-C6, waiter's tip posture, grasp preserved
  • Klumpke: C8-T1, claw hand, may have Horner syndrome
  • Treatment: brief immobilization, then physiotherapy
  • No biceps recovery after months: surgical referral
  • Clavicle fracture: crepitus at the clavicle, also conservative
exam_pearl: Erb palsy is managed conservatively first; surgery only if recovery fails over months.

stem: A mother of a 2-month-old infant complains that her baby has frequent episodes of excessive crying, often lasting about 3 hours, during which the baby raises legs and passes gas. The baby has normal growth and feeding. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: excessive crying, often lasting about 3 hours
why_right: Recurrent bouts of crying lasting "about 3 hours" in a "2-month-old" who draws up the legs and passes gas, with "normal growth and feeding", is infantile colic. Colic is benign and self-limited, usually settling by 3 to 4 months, so management is reassurance of the parents plus soothing and behavioural strategies. No drug or investigation is needed when the baby is thriving.
why_wrong_block:
B. Option not given in this recall. Common distractors here are formula change (only if features of cow's milk protein allergy such as vomiting, bloody stool or poor growth) or colic drops.
C. Simethicone has no proven benefit over placebo in colic; the gas is a result of crying and swallowed air, not the cause, so medication is not the most appropriate management.
D. Option not given in this recall. Any investigation or referral would only be indicated with red flags (fever, vomiting, poor weight gain, abnormal exam).
key_concept:
Colic = rule of 3s in a well, growing infant: reassure and support parents.
  • Crying ≥3 h/day, ≥3 days/week, ≥3 weeks
  • Onset in first weeks, peaks around 6 weeks, resolves by 3 to 4 months
  • Treatment: reassurance, soothing (holding, rocking, swaddling, white noise), parental support
  • Not recommended: simethicone, anticholinergic drops, routine formula switch
  • Red flags that change the answer: fever, vomiting, blood in stool, poor growth
exam_pearl: Normal growth and feeding is the clue that rules out organic causes; with that clue, any drug option is a distractor.

stem: A 4-year-old child presents with nocturnal cough. I think he had URTI before. But he have similar episodes of the cough not preceded by URTI and relieved by inhaler What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: similar episodes of the cough not preceded by URTI
why_right: Recurrent "nocturnal cough" in a "4-year-old", including episodes "not preceded by URTI" and "relieved by inhaler", is a picture of asthma (the other version adds eczema and expiratory wheeze). In children under 5, diagnosis is clinical and based on response to treatment, because spirometry is not reliably performed at this age. Recurrent persistent symptoms with night waking justify a controller: a trial of low-dose inhaled corticosteroid.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chest X-ray is not needed for typical asthma; it is used when a foreign body, pneumonia or a structural lesion is suspected (focal signs, sudden onset, fever).
B. Spirometry confirms asthma in children about 6 years and older and adults; a 4-year-old usually cannot perform reproducible forced manoeuvres, so a therapeutic trial is used instead.
key_concept:
Under 5 with recurrent wheeze or night cough responsive to bronchodilator: treat as asthma clinically.
  • Under 5: diagnosis by pattern + response to SABA/ICS trial
  • ≥6 years: spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility
  • Night symptoms or frequent reliever use = uncontrolled, add ICS
  • Atopy (eczema) strengthens the diagnosis
  • CXR only for atypical features or suspected foreign body
exam_pearl: Age decides the fork: a 4-year-old gets an ICS trial, an older child or adult would get spirometry first.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): 4-year-old boy with history of eczema, cough following URTI, similar episode recently without URTI relieved by inhaler, bilateral expiratory wheezes; management? A. Chest X-ray, B. Spirometry, C. Chest CT, D. Inhaled corticosteroids (highlighted).

stem: child comes with abdominal pain, bringing his legs to chest and has red currant jelly stool. What is the best way to prevent this occurrence?
why_right: Colicky pain with legs drawn to the chest and "red currant jelly stool" is intussusception. This recall's key is exclusive breastfeeding, reflecting the view that breastfeeding is protective against intussusception (it reduces gut infections that cause lymphoid hyperplasia, the usual lead point in idiopathic cases). Among the options listed it is the only one framed as primary prevention in infancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Early symptom education does not prevent intussusception from happening; it allows earlier presentation and enema reduction before ischaemia (it is the key in the 3-option version of this recall).
B. High fiber diet prevents constipation, not intussusception, and is not relevant to infants in the typical age group.
C. Physical activity has no role in preventing intussusception.
key_concept:
Intussusception: colicky pain + legs drawn up + currant jelly stool + sausage mass.
  • Peak age 6 months to 3 years; most idiopathic (lymphoid hyperplasia after viral infection)
  • Diagnosis: ultrasound (target/doughnut sign)
  • Treatment: IV fluids, then air or contrast enema reduction
  • Surgery: peritonitis, perforation, failed enema
  • Recurrence is more common after enema than after surgery
exam_pearl: Check which options are present: with exclusive breastfeeding listed, this recall keys it; when it is absent, the key becomes educating about early symptoms.

stem: child comes with abdominal pain, bringing his legs to chest and has red currant jelly stool. What is the best way to prevent this occurrence?
why_right: Colicky pain with legs drawn to the chest and "red currant jelly stool" is intussusception, which is mostly idiopathic and has no reliable primary prevention. What parents can do is recognise early symptoms (paroxysmal crying with legs drawn up, vomiting, bloody stool, lethargy) and seek care fast, so enema reduction is done before bowel ischaemia, perforation or shock, and recurrences are caught early.
why_wrong_block:
B. High fiber diet prevents constipation, not intussusception; it has no effect on the lymphoid lead points behind idiopathic cases.
C. Physical activity in infancy has no role in preventing intussusception or its complications.
key_concept:
When a disease cannot be prevented, "prevention" in the stem means preventing complications by early recognition.
  • Intussusception peak age 6 months to 3 years
  • Early signs: paroxysmal colicky crying, legs drawn up, vomiting, lethargy
  • Late signs: currant jelly stool, shock, peritonitis
  • Early enema reduction avoids surgery and bowel resection
  • Recurrence occurs, mostly after enema reduction
exam_pearl: A 4-option version adds exclusive breastfeeding and is keyed to it; in this 3-option version, educate about early symptoms is the key.

stem: Case of pyloric stenosis What is the most important protective or preventive measures from parents
highlight_terms_source: protective or preventive measures from parents
why_right: Pyloric stenosis is a hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle with no known primary prevention, so the most useful parental measure is to know the early symptoms: non-bilious projectile vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks, a hungry baby after vomiting, and poor weight gain. Early presentation allows diagnosis by ultrasound and pyloromyotomy before severe dehydration and hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis develop. This matters especially for later siblings, since there is a familial tendency.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fiber intake is irrelevant in a young infant and treats constipation, not a gastric outlet obstruction.
C. Anti reflux medications treat GERD (effortless, non-projectile regurgitation in a thriving baby); they neither prevent nor treat pyloric muscle hypertrophy.
key_concept:
Pyloric stenosis: projectile non-bilious vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks, hungry after feeds, olive mass.
  • Risk: male, first born, family history
  • Labs: hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Diagnosis: abdominal ultrasound
  • Treatment: correct fluids and electrolytes first, then pyloromyotomy
  • No primary prevention: educate for early recognition
exam_pearl: Projectile, non-bilious, hungry baby = pyloric stenosis; effortless spitting in a thriving baby = reflux, where reassurance fits instead.

stem: A child with cystic fibrosis (CF) is brought to your clinic. The mother asks: "Is it safe for my child to play with another child who also has cystic fibrosis?" What is the best advice?
OptA: Yes, it is safe; they can play together freely
OptB: No, avoid close contact with each other to prevent cross-infection
OptC: Only if both children are on antibiotics
highlight_terms_source: play with another child who also has cystic fibrosis
why_right: Children with cystic fibrosis carry organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Burkholderia cepacia that spread easily between CF patients and cause rapid lung decline. Infection control guidance therefore advises that people with CF avoid close contact with each other (keep a physical distance, do not share equipment or play closely), so the answer to "is it safe to play together?" is no.
why_wrong_block:
A. Free play allows droplet and contact spread of CF pathogens between patients, which is exactly what cross-infection guidance aims to prevent.
C. Being on antibiotics does not eradicate colonisation or make contact safe; resistant organisms can still be transmitted.
D. Masks reduce but do not eliminate transmission and do not address contact spread; the recommendation is to avoid close contact altogether.
key_concept:
CF to CF cross-infection: keep CF patients apart.
  • Key organisms: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Burkholderia cepacia complex, MRSA, nontuberculous mycobacteria
  • Advice: avoid close contact, keep distance, no sharing of devices or toys
  • Clinics separate CF patients in time and space
  • Contact with non-CF children is fine with good hand hygiene
exam_pearl: The risk is CF to CF, not CF to healthy children; the CF child can attend school and play with non-CF peers.

stem: 7yo female cystic fibrosis , playing with other child with cystic fibrosis , most appropriate?
OptB: influenza vaccine for both of them
highlight_terms_source: playing with other child with cystic fibrosis
why_right: A "7yo" with cystic fibrosis "playing with other child with cystic fibrosis" is at risk of cross-infection with organisms like Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Burkholderia cepacia, which are transmitted between CF patients and accelerate lung damage. The most appropriate action is to separate them and advise that CF patients avoid close contact with one another.
why_wrong_block:
A. Masks lower but do not remove the risk, and close play still allows contact transmission; segregation is the recommendation.
B. Annual influenza vaccine is recommended for every CF patient, but it does not protect against bacterial cross-infection such as Pseudomonas or Burkholderia.
key_concept:
Two CF patients together: separate them (cross-infection control).
  • Transmissible: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Burkholderia cepacia complex, MRSA
  • Avoid close contact and shared equipment between CF patients
  • Influenza vaccine: yearly for all CF patients, but a separate issue
exam_pearl: Influenza vaccine is right when the stem asks how to reduce infections at school; it is wrong when the stem is about two CF children together.

stem: child with cystic fibrosis came with recurrent Pulmonary Infections Despite respiratory clearance and he well start to go school this year what should do to decrease the incidence of recurrent infection ?
why_right: A CF child with "recurrent pulmonary infections despite respiratory clearance" who will "start to go school" faces more viral exposure, and influenza triggers pulmonary exacerbations in CF. Annual inactivated influenza vaccination (for the patient and household) is a standard recommendation that reduces these infections without restricting normal life.
why_wrong_block:
A. Keeping the child out of school is not recommended; CF children should attend school with hand hygiene and vaccination, and only contact with other CF patients is restricted.
B. The stem says infections recur "despite respiratory clearance", so simply increasing airway clearance does not address the new exposure risk at school.
key_concept:
CF infection prevention: vaccinate, airway clearance, hygiene, separate from other CF patients.
  • Annual inactivated influenza vaccine from 6 months of age, plus household contacts
  • Complete routine schedule including pneumococcal vaccines
  • Daily airway clearance and inhaled therapies
  • Hand hygiene; avoid close contact with other CF patients
exam_pearl: Despite clearance + new school exposure points to vaccination, not isolation or more of the same therapy.

stem: A 9-year-old child presents with mild bilateral leg pain that has been gradually increasing over the past 3 months. He has spent less time in outdoor activities recently and reports feeling fatigued after walking short distances. Patient has good diet and appetite. Physical examination normal. Your next step
OptB: Advise increase in outdoor activities and play .
OptC: Advise sun exposure and vitamin D supplements
highlight_terms_source: spent less time in outdoor activities
why_right: Gradually increasing "bilateral leg pain" over "3 months", "less time in outdoor activities" and fatigue on walking, with a "normal" exam, suggest nutritional vitamin D deficiency from low sun exposure. "Good diet and appetite" makes malnutrition or malabsorption unlikely, so lack of sunlight is the cause. This recall's key is calcium plus vitamin D, because symptomatic vitamin D deficiency in children is treated with vitamin D given together with calcium to restore bone mineralisation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Orthopedic referral is for structural or red flag problems (limp, swelling, deformity, night pain with systemic signs, abnormal exam); the exam here is normal.
B. Outdoor play alone does not treat an established deficiency causing symptoms for 3 months; it is supportive advice only.
C. Close, and sun exposure is sound advice, but the keyed choice pairs vitamin D with calcium; treatment of symptomatic deficiency bone disease combines both, even when the diet seems adequate.
key_concept:
Bone pain + low sun exposure in a child = think vitamin D deficiency.
  • Young child: rickets (bowed legs, widened wrists, delayed walking)
  • Older child: diffuse bone pain, muscle weakness, fatigue
  • Confirm: 25-OH vitamin D, calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH
  • Treat: vitamin D with calcium, plus sun exposure advice
  • Growing pains: night pain, normal daytime activity, no fatigue
exam_pearl: Reduced outdoor time is the hidden clue for vitamin D; normal exam with gradual pain and fatigue argues against an orthopedic cause.

stem: A 3-year-old child presents with poor feeding and hematuria. On examination, there is a large abdominal mass, and chest examination shows decreased air entry in multiple areas. What is the most important investigation in the disease assessment?
highlight_terms_source: decreased air entry in multiple areas
why_right: A "3-year-old" with "hematuria" and a "large abdominal mass" is Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma); "decreased air entry in multiple areas" suggests lung metastases, the commonest site of spread. Abdominal ultrasound is the key first investigation to confirm the mass arises from the kidney, assess the other kidney, and check the renal vein and IVC for tumour thrombus, before CT for staging.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chest CT is used for staging lung metastases once Wilms is established, but it does not characterise the primary abdominal mass.
B. Bone marrow aspiration is part of staging neuroblastoma (which spreads to marrow and bone); Wilms rarely involves the marrow, and hematuria points to a renal origin.
key_concept:
Abdominal mass in a young child: Wilms vs neuroblastoma.
  • Wilms: 2 to 5 years, smooth flank mass not crossing midline, hematuria, hypertension, lung metastases
  • Neuroblastoma: younger, crosses midline, calcified, raised urinary catecholamines, bone and marrow spread
  • First test: abdominal ultrasound; then CT abdomen and chest for staging
  • Do not palpate repeatedly (risk of rupture)
exam_pearl: Hematuria plus abdominal mass = Wilms, so image the kidney first; marrow aspiration belongs to neuroblastoma or leukemia.

stem: A 12-year-old boy is diagnosed with stage 1 hypertension during a routine checkup. His blood pressure readings have been consistently elevated on multiple occasions. He is otherwise healthy with a normal BMI and no signs of end-organ damage. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: This recall's key is renal ultrasound because hypertension in a child is more often secondary than in adults, and the renal parenchyma is the commonest source; a "12-year-old" with confirmed ("consistently elevated on multiple occasions") stage 1 hypertension and a "normal BMI" has no obesity to explain it, so the source sends him to look for a renal cause. Lifestyle advice still runs alongside the work-up.
why_wrong_block:
A. An ACE inhibitor is not first for uncomplicated stage 1 hypertension with no end-organ damage; drugs are added for symptomatic or stage 2 hypertension, CKD or diabetes, target organ damage, or failure of lifestyle measures.
B. Lifestyle modification (diet, exercise, salt reduction) is the first treatment for stage 1 hypertension in any child; this card's key prefers the secondary-cause work-up because he is young and not obese.
D. Smoking cessation is only relevant if he smokes; nothing in the stem suggests tobacco use, so it is not the next step.
key_concept:
Pediatric hypertension: confirm it, look for a cause, treat with lifestyle first.
  • Confirm on repeated visits; ABPM to exclude white coat hypertension
  • Younger age, non obese, or abnormal urinalysis/renal function: think secondary (renal parenchymal, renovascular)
  • Renal ultrasound: targeted test for suspected renal cause
  • Stage 1, no organ damage: lifestyle modification first
  • Drugs: symptomatic, stage 2, CKD/diabetes, LVH, or lifestyle failure
exam_pearl: If the stem gives an obese teenager with a family history, the answer flips to lifestyle modification rather than a secondary-cause search.

stem: A 12-year-old boy is diagnosed with stage 1 hypertension during a routine checkup. His blood pressure readings have been consistently elevated on multiple occasions. He is otherwise healthy with a normal BMI and no signs of end-organ damage. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is the step that confirms true hypertension before any secondary work-up or treatment. Office readings in a "12-year-old" who is "otherwise healthy" with "no signs of end-organ damage" can be inflated by white coat effect, and ABPM is recommended in children with persistent stage 1 readings to confirm the diagnosis and its severity.
why_wrong_block:
B. Renal ultrasound with Doppler looks for renal parenchymal or renovascular disease; it is ordered once hypertension is confirmed and a secondary cause is suspected (young age, abnormal urinalysis, bruit).
C. Catecholamines (metanephrines) test for pheochromocytoma, which needs paroxysms of headache, sweating and palpitations; he has none.
D. The renin to aldosterone ratio screens for primary hyperaldosteronism, suggested by hypokalemia or resistant hypertension, which are absent here.
key_concept:
Pediatric hypertension: confirm before you chase a cause.
  • Elevated office readings on repeated visits: confirm with ABPM
  • ABPM separates white coat from true and masked hypertension
  • Renal US with Doppler: suspected renal or renovascular cause
  • Metanephrines: paroxysmal symptoms (pheochromocytoma)
  • Renin/aldosterone: hypokalemia or resistant hypertension
exam_pearl: When the options are all investigations and nothing points to a specific secondary cause, the answer is the test that confirms the hypertension itself (ABPM).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Second version (Q) under 577 with a different option set.

stem: 13- years old female presented with chronic diarrhoea and altered bowel habits for 3-4 months, did colonoscopy: showed transmural inflamed patches, what is the first-option treatment?
why_right: Chronic diarrhoea for months with "transmural inflamed patches" (skip lesions, full thickness inflammation) is Crohn's disease. To induce remission of active luminal disease, systemic corticosteroids are the classic first option among these choices; they act quickly but are not used for maintenance.
why_wrong_block:
B. Infliximab (anti-TNF) is for fistulizing or perianal disease, severe or high-risk disease, or steroid refractory/dependent cases, not the routine first option for uncomplicated luminal Crohn's.
C. Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing maintenance agent; it is slow in onset and not used to induce remission first.
D. This is a placeholder from the recaller, not a treatment option.
key_concept:
Crohn's disease: induce, then maintain.
  • Transmural, patchy (skip) inflammation, often terminal ileum: Crohn's
  • Induction, pediatric: exclusive enteral nutrition or corticosteroids
  • Maintenance: azathioprine or methotrexate
  • Fistulizing/perianal or severe disease: anti-TNF (infliximab)
  • Steroids never for maintenance
exam_pearl: If "exclusive enteral nutrition" or "manage nutrition" is offered in a child with luminal Crohn's, it is the preferred first-line induction over steroids.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q): patient complaining of abdominal (pain); microscopic finding transmural patchy at terminal ileum (diagnosis not written); management: manage nutrition / methotrexate / infliximab / steroid (no mark).

stem: A full-term infant of a diabetic mother has a hematocrit of 71% and appears plethoric. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: An infant of a diabetic mother with a hematocrit of 71% and plethora has neonatal polycythemia (venous hematocrit above 65%). The stem gives no symptoms of hyperviscosity (no lethargy, respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia or seizures), so management is hydration with IV fluids and monitoring; partial exchange is kept for symptomatic infants.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance alone ignores a hematocrit well above the polycythemia threshold; the baby needs hydration and monitoring for hyperviscosity complications.
B. Partial exchange transfusion with saline is for symptomatic polycythemia (hyperviscosity signs) or very high hematocrits; plethora alone is a sign of polycythemia, not a hyperviscosity symptom.
C. Phototherapy treats hyperbilirubinemia; polycythemia raises the jaundice risk, but there is no jaundice here and it does not lower the hematocrit.
key_concept:
Neonatal polycythemia: venous hematocrit above 65%.
  • Causes: infant of diabetic mother, IUGR, delayed cord clamping, twin to twin transfusion
  • Signs: plethora, lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia, jaundice
  • Asymptomatic: IV fluids/hydration and monitoring
  • Symptomatic (hyperviscosity): partial exchange transfusion
  • Always check glucose in an IDM
exam_pearl: Plethora is not a symptom; if the stem adds lethargy, seizures, respiratory distress or hypoglycaemia, the answer flips to partial exchange transfusion.

stem: An 18-month-old child with normal growth and weight is brought by his parents. They are concerned because his older sibling has celiac disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: This recall's key is reassurance because the 18-month-old is asymptomatic with normal growth (50th percentile); a sibling's diagnosis raises risk but does not make this child ill. Screening of well first-degree relatives is usually deferred until about 2 to 3 years of age, after adequate gluten exposure, so nothing is needed today beyond reassurance and a plan to test later or sooner if symptoms appear. A gluten free diet must never be started without a confirmed diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. tTG-IgA (with total IgA) is the right first test when there are celiac symptoms (diarrhea, distension, failure to thrive), or as screening of an at-risk relative once older (about 2 to 3 years); this toddler is well and young, so testing can wait.
C. Starting a gluten free diet without serology and biopsy is wrong: it is unnecessary in a healthy child and causes false negative results if testing is later needed.
key_concept:
Celiac disease workup:
  • Symptoms or failure to thrive: tTG-IgA (with total IgA) while on gluten
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (do not stop gluten before)
  • Treatment: gluten free diet only after diagnosis
  • At-risk groups: first-degree relatives, type 1 diabetes, Down, Turner syndromes
exam_pearl: Never start a gluten free diet before testing; it masks the diagnosis.

stem: An 4-Year-Old child with normal growth and weight is brought by his parents. They are concerned because his older sibling has celiac disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: First-degree relatives of a patient with celiac disease are at high risk and should be screened even when asymptomatic. This child with "normal growth and weight" whose "older sibling has celiac disease" should have tTG IgA, the initial screening serology, while still eating gluten.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance misses a high-risk child; normal growth does not exclude celiac disease, which can be silent in relatives.
C. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing is wrong: gluten withdrawal makes serology and biopsy falsely negative, and diet is only started after the diagnosis is confirmed.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: serology, then biopsy, then diet.
  • Screen first-degree relatives and type 1 diabetes even without symptoms
  • Initial test: tTG IgA (with total IgA)
  • Confirm: endoscopy with duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia)
  • Test while on gluten
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten-free diet; tTG also monitors compliance
exam_pearl: Never start a gluten-free diet before serology and biopsy; it produces false-negative results.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2112).

stem: A case of hemolytic uremic syndrome diarrhea. Lab investigations was ordered. What are findings?
why_right: Diarrhea-associated HUS (Shiga toxin E. coli O157:H7) causes a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia: red cells are sheared in small vessels, producing fragmented RBCs (schistocytes) on the smear. Together with thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury this forms the HUS triad.
why_wrong_block:
A. Atypical lymphocytes are the smear finding of infectious mononucleosis (EBV), not HUS.
B. Eosinophilia suggests parasitic infection, allergy or drug reaction; it is not a feature of HUS.
key_concept:
HUS triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury.
  • Classic: child under 5 after bloody diarrhea (E. coli O157:H7, Shiga toxin)
  • Smear: schistocytes (helmet cells)
  • Schistocytes also in TTP, DIC, HELLP, mechanical valves
  • Treatment: supportive; avoid antibiotics
  • Most common cause of acute renal failure in children
exam_pearl: Fever and neurological signs in an adult with the same smear point to TTP (low ADAMTS13), not HUS.

stem: Pediatric with KNEE AND ANKLE (2 Joints) pain, limited range of motion, warmth, had gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago US shows effusion. How to MANAGE (It was management)
OptC: synovial aspiration for analysis and culture
why_right: Pain and swelling in two lower limb joints ("KNEE AND ANKLE") "2 weeks" after gastroenteritis is post-enteric reactive arthritis: a sterile, oligoarticular inflammatory arthritis. The effusion is sterile inflammation, and first-line treatment is an NSAID such as oral ibuprofen.
why_wrong_block:
B. Aspirin is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome risk; it is reserved for specific indications such as Kawasaki disease.
C. Synovial aspiration is the step for a single hot joint with fever or systemic toxicity where septic arthritis must be excluded; here two joints (oligoarticular) 2 weeks after an enteric infection, without fever, fits reactive arthritis.
D. IV antibiotics treat septic arthritis (usually one joint, febrile, toxic child), after aspiration and cultures; reactive arthritis is sterile.
key_concept:
Joint pain after infection in a child: count the joints and check for fever.
  • 2 or more joints, 1 to 4 weeks after gastroenteritis or urethritis: reactive arthritis, NSAID
  • Single hot joint, fever, refusal to move: septic arthritis, aspirate then IV antibiotics
  • Hip pain after viral URTI, well child: transient synovitis
  • Migratory arthritis after sore throat: acute rheumatic fever
exam_pearl: One joint plus fever flips the answer to synovial aspiration for analysis and culture.

stem: Pediatric with knee pain, limited range of motion, warmth, had gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago Xray shows No effusion How to MANAGE (It was management)
OptC: synovial aspiration for analysis and culture
why_right: This recall's key is synovial aspiration because a single warm knee with "limited range of motion" in a child is septic arthritis until proven otherwise, and joint fluid analysis with culture is the test that confirms or excludes it. Plain X-ray is insensitive for effusion, so "no effusion" on X-ray does not rule out a septic joint.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral ibuprofen treats reactive arthritis or transient synovitis, but only after septic arthritis is excluded in a monoarticular hot joint.
B. Aspirin is avoided in children (Reye syndrome) and does not address the need to exclude infection.
D. IV antibiotics are started for suspected septic arthritis, ideally after aspiration and cultures are taken; the diagnostic step comes first here.
key_concept:
Monoarticular hot joint in a child: exclude septic arthritis first.
  • Features: fever, warm tender joint, reduced ROM, refusal to bear weight
  • Ultrasound detects effusion better than X-ray
  • Key test: arthrocentesis with cell count, Gram stain and culture, plus blood culture
  • Most common organism: Staphylococcus aureus
  • Then empirical IV antibiotics
exam_pearl: Compare the paired card: two joints after gastroenteritis is reactive arthritis treated with ibuprofen; a single hot joint is aspirated.

stem: A 6 months old child known case cerebral palsy With recurrent episodes of pneumonia (Did They Say Aspiration?) And Failure To Thrive Despite Thickened Formula. Diagnosis of GERD is suspected. What is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?
highlight_terms_source: Failure To Thrive Despite Thickened Formula
why_right: This recall's key is a contrast upper GI study because this neurologically impaired infant has complicated reflux ("recurrent episodes of pneumonia", "failure to thrive despite thickened formula") and is heading towards surgical anti-reflux management. The contrast study shows anatomy (malrotation, hiatal hernia, stricture, obstruction) that can mimic or worsen GERD and is required before fundoplication.
why_wrong_block:
B. pH (or pH impedance) monitoring quantifies reflux and links it to symptoms such as cough or apnea; it confirms GERD but does not show the anatomy needed before surgery.
C. Endoscopy with biopsy assesses esophagitis, strictures or eosinophilic esophagitis; it is invasive and not the first study here.
D. A PPI trial is for uncomplicated symptoms in older children; in infants it is not a diagnostic test, and with aspiration pneumonias and failure to thrive objective evaluation is needed.
key_concept:
Infant GERD: physiological reflux vs complicated GERD.
  • Happy spitter, gaining weight: reassurance, feeding advice
  • Red flags: failure to thrive, recurrent pneumonia, apnea, Sandifer posturing
  • Contrast upper GI study: anatomy (malrotation, hiatal hernia, stricture), pre-surgery
  • pH impedance: quantify reflux, correlate with symptoms
  • Endoscopy: esophagitis or other mucosal disease
  • Cerebral palsy with refractory GERD: fundoplication with or without gastrostomy
exam_pearl: If the question asks for the most accurate test to confirm reflux itself, the answer is pH impedance monitoring, not the contrast study.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller note: this is the full recall in this exact order.

stem: A previously healthy 4-month-old uncircumcised boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fever. He has not had vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or nasal congestion. There has been no known contact with ill persons. He has continued to breastfeed and has not had a decrease in the number wet diapers. He is mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive. Examination shows no focus of infection. Urinary catheterization is performed (see lab results). Temperature 39.1 °C. Test Result Normal Values: pH 7.5 (4.3-8); Specific gravity 1010 (1001-1030); Protein Absent (Absent); Glucose Absent (Absent); Ketones Absent (Absent); Nitrite Positive (Absent); Leukocytes 30-40 (0-3 per high power field); Erythrocytes 5-10 (0-2 per high power field). Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical therapy?
highlight_terms_source: mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive
why_right: Positive nitrite with 30 to 40 leukocytes on a catheter sample in a febrile "uncircumcised" infant means febrile UTI. He is beyond the young infant age, "mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive", still breastfeeding with normal wet diapers, so he tolerates oral intake and can be treated with an oral agent such as cephalexin, which is as effective as IV therapy in this setting.
why_wrong_block:
B. Azithromycin (a macrolide) does not cover E. coli and other Gram negative uropathogens and has no role in UTI.
C. Cefepime is a broad spectrum antipseudomonal agent for hospital-acquired or resistant infections; a mild community UTI does not need it.
D. IV ceftriaxone is for infants under about 2 months, toxic appearance, vomiting or inability to take oral medication; none applies here.
key_concept:
Febrile UTI in infants: oral vs IV.
  • Diagnosis: catheter or suprapubic sample; nitrite and leukocytes support, culture confirms
  • Oral (cephalexin, cefixime, amoxicillin-clavulanate): well appearing, tolerating orals
  • IV (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime): young infants, toxic, vomiting, cannot take orals
  • Risk factors: uncircumcised male, fever ≥39 °C, VUR, constipation
exam_pearl: Add vomiting, toxic appearance or age under 2 months and the answer flips to IV ceftriaxone.

stem: A previously healthy 4-month-old uncircumcised boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fever. He has not had vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or nasal congestion. There has been no known contact with ill persons. He has continued to breastfeed and has not had a decrease in the number wet diapers. He is mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive. Examination shows no focus of infection. Urinary catheterization is performed (see lab results). Temperature 39.1 °C. Test Result Normal Values: pH 7.5 (4.3-8); Specific gravity 1010 (1001-1030); Protein Absent (Absent); Glucose Absent (Absent); Ketones Absent (Absent); Nitrite Positive (Absent); Leukocytes 30-40 (0-3 per high power field); Erythrocytes 5-10 (0-2 per high power field). Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical therapy?
highlight_terms_source: mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive
why_right: The decisive point is the route: a 4-month-old who is "mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive", still breastfeeding and with normal wet diapers can take oral medication, so an oral antibiotic is appropriate. The catheter sample (nitrite positive, leukocytes 30-40/HPF) supports a febrile UTI in an uncircumcised boy, and oral therapy works as well as IV in a non-toxic infant older than about 2 months. This recall's key is the oral option, recorded here as amoxicillin.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral azithromycin: a macrolide with poor activity against E. coli and other Gram-negative uropathogens; it is used for atypical respiratory infections, not UTI.
C. IV cefepime: a broad-spectrum antipseudomonal agent kept for complicated, hospital-acquired or resistant infections; far too broad and needlessly IV for a mild community UTI.
D. IV ceftriaxone: right if the infant were under about 2 months, toxic looking, vomiting or unable to take oral fluids; this baby is alert and feeding.
key_concept:
Febrile UTI in infants: the route depends on age and how ill the child looks.
  • Over ~2 months, non-toxic, tolerating oral intake: oral antibiotic (cephalexin, cefixime, amoxicillin-clavulanate, per local susceptibility)
  • Under ~2 months, toxic, vomiting or unable to drink: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime
  • UA support: pyuria, positive nitrite, positive leukocyte esterase
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by urine culture from catheter or suprapubic aspiration
  • Uncircumcised male infants are at higher risk
exam_pearl: "Alert, feeding, normal wet diapers" means oral; "toxic, vomiting or under 2 months" means IV ceftriaxone.

stem: Child with constipation and symptoms of cystitis/UTI. Most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
why_right: The child has "symptoms of cystitis/UTI", which need an antibiotic active against E. coli, and amoxicillin is the oral option offered. Constipation is a recognized risk factor for UTI because it impairs bladder emptying; it explains why the infection happened but does not change the need to treat it. Constipation should also be managed to prevent recurrence. Option C was not recorded.
why_wrong_block:
B. Metronidazole: covers anaerobes and protozoa (C. difficile, Giardia, bacterial vaginosis), not the Gram-negative organisms that cause UTI; constipation is not an infection to treat.
D. No treatment: right only for asymptomatic bacteriuria in a healthy child; a symptomatic UTI must be treated to relieve symptoms and prevent pyelonephritis and renal scarring.
key_concept:
Constipation + UTI: treat the infection AND the bowel.
  • UTI risk factors: constipation, VUR, posterior urethral valves, uncircumcised male infant, incomplete bladder emptying
  • Symptomatic UTI: oral antibiotic (amoxicillin if susceptible, cefixime, TMP-SMX, nitrofurantoin)
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a healthy child: no antibiotics
  • Treat constipation to reduce recurrences
exam_pearl: Constipation is a risk factor, not an indication for metronidazole; the UTI still needs a urinary antibiotic.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option C not recorded.

stem: A newborn presents with persistent bleeding after circumcision that does not stop with compression. There is a positive family history of a bleeding disorder affecting Mother's Brother (no labs). What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Two clues settle it: bleeding after circumcision in a newborn (a classic first sign of severe hemophilia) and a bleeding disorder in the mother's brother. An affected maternal uncle means an X-linked recessive pattern: the mother is a carrier and her son is affected. Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is the most common X-linked bleeding disorder, so it is the most likely diagnosis. Expected labs: prolonged aPTT with normal PT and platelet count.
why_wrong_block:
B. Von Willebrand disease: usually autosomal dominant, affects both sexes and passes through either parent. It typically causes mild mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gums, menorrhagia) and rarely severe neonatal circumcision bleeding; it fits best with mucosal bleeding and a parent of either sex affected.
C. DIC: secondary to a severe illness (sepsis, asphyxia, shock) in a sick neonate who bleeds from many sites; it is not inherited and would not explain a family history.
D. Platelet disorder: causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding, and most inherited platelet function disorders are autosomal; it fits best with petechiae or a low platelet count, not an X-linked history with circumcision bleeding.
key_concept:
Bleeding pattern + inheritance identifies the disorder.
  • Maternal uncle or male relatives on the mother's side affected: X-linked, so hemophilia A (VIII) or B (IX)
  • Hemophilia: prolonged aPTT, normal PT and platelets; deep bleeding (joints, muscles, circumcision)
  • VWD: autosomal, mucosal bleeding, normal or mildly prolonged aPTT, prolonged bleeding time
  • Platelet disorders: petechiae, mucosal bleeding
  • DIC: sick patient, prolonged PT and aPTT, low platelets and fibrinogen
exam_pearl: "Mother's brother" means X-linked, so hemophilia; mucosal bleeding with both sexes affected suggests VWD.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0374 → B. Von Willebrand disease. Confirm before the exam.

stem: Pediatric patient was brought to ED with decreased level of consciousness. BP 75/55 HR 300/min ECG picture: SVT Whats the appropriate immediate management?
why_right: The child is unstable: "decreased level of consciousness" and BP 75/55 with SVT at 300/min. In any tachyarrhythmia the first question is stability, and unstable SVT is treated with immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion. Drugs and vagal maneuvers are steps for the stable patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amiodarone: a second-line antiarrhythmic for refractory SVT in a stable child, usually with expert advice; it is slow to act and can worsen hypotension.
B. Vagal maneuvers: the first step in a stable child with SVT (ice to the face in infants, Valsalva in older children); they waste time in a child with altered consciousness and hypotension.
C. Adenosine: the drug of choice for stable SVT after vagal maneuvers fail; in an unstable child it may be tried only if IV access is already in place and it causes no delay, but cardioversion is the standard answer when consciousness is impaired.
key_concept:
SVT ladder: check stability first.
  • Unstable (hypotension, altered consciousness, shock, heart failure): synchronized cardioversion
  • Stable: vagal maneuvers first
  • Then adenosine (rapid push, escalating dose)
  • Then other agents (CCB in older patients, amiodarone or procainamide in children) or cardioversion
  • Avoid verapamil in infants
exam_pearl: Same ECG, different answer: an alert child with normal BP gets vagal maneuvers or adenosine; drowsy and hypotensive gets synchronized cardioversion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version: An 8-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department. He is alert, with BP 75/50 mmHg and HR 130/min. His ECG is shown (narrow complex tachycardia). Options Adenosine / Amiodarone / Vagal stimulation / Synchronized electrical cardioversion; D highlighted. Answer D: Unstable px with SVT.

stem: Child with a known fatty acid oxidation defect (detoxification) develops fatigue and hypoglycemia following a viral illness. Which of the following measures is most effective in preventing metabolic decompensation during future illness episodes?
why_right: Fatty acid oxidation defects prevent the body from using fat for energy and ketones during fasting or catabolic stress, so illness causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia and metabolic crisis. The key to prevention is to avoid fasting and supply carbohydrate during illness: a sick-day plan of frequent glucose-containing feeds, with early IV dextrose (continuous glucose infusion) if the child cannot take orals. A steady glucose supply suppresses lipolysis and prevents decompensation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fasting to promote ketone production: the opposite of correct; these children cannot oxidize fat to make ketones, so fasting is the trigger for hypoglycemia and crisis.
C. High-fat diet: increases the load on the defective pathway; long-chain defects are managed with a low long-chain fat diet, often supplemented with MCT.
D. Protein restriction: the mainstay for urea cycle disorders and organic acidemias (hyperammonemia), not for fatty acid oxidation defects.
key_concept:
Fatty acid oxidation defect (e.g. MCAD): never let them fast.
  • Crisis: hypoketotic hypoglycemia after fasting or viral illness, lethargy, possible hepatomegaly and cardiomyopathy
  • Prevention: frequent feeds, avoid prolonged fasting, sick-day carbohydrate plan
  • Unable to take orals: early IV dextrose infusion
  • Long-chain defects: restrict long-chain fat, use MCT
  • Urea cycle defects / organic acidemias: protein restriction
exam_pearl: Hypoglycemia WITHOUT ketones after fasting or illness suggests a fatty acid oxidation defect: give glucose, never fast.

stem: A school-aged child with asthma came to the ER with acute asthma exacerbation, SpO2 95%, peak flow meter at best 60, can complete full sentences, took two puffs of salbutamol at home, mild wheeze on auscultation. Which is the most appropriate management?
OptD: Give salbutamol by spacer then reassess
why_right: This is a mild to moderate exacerbation: SpO2 95% (above 92%), "can complete full sentences" and only "mild wheeze", and a peak flow of about 60% of best is above the 50% cut-off for a severe attack. The first step is an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist given by spacer (as effective as a nebulizer in mild/moderate attacks), followed by reassessment of symptoms and peak flow to decide what comes next.
why_wrong_block:
A. Start oral corticosteroids and hospitalize: hospitalization is for severe or life-threatening attacks (SpO2 below 92%, too breathless to talk, poor response to bronchodilators). Systemic steroids are part of exacerbation care, but this child needs bronchodilator and reassessment first, not admission.
B. Add salmeterol and hospitalize: salmeterol is a long-acting controller with slow onset, not a reliever, and is never used alone in asthma; admission is not indicated for a mild attack.
C. Add ipratropium: added to repeated salbutamol in severe or life-threatening exacerbations or poor response to SABA, not as the first step in a mild attack.
key_concept:
Acute asthma in children: classify severity, then treat.
  • Mild/moderate: SpO2 above 92%, talks in full sentences, minimal accessory muscle use: SABA via spacer, reassess
  • Severe: SpO2 below 92%, too breathless to talk or feed, PEFR 33-50%: oxygen, repeated SABA + ipratropium, systemic steroids
  • Life-threatening: silent chest, cyanosis, altered consciousness, PEFR below 33%: add IV magnesium, ICU
  • Order: oxygen if needed, SABA, systemic steroids, reassess, escalate
exam_pearl: Full sentences and SpO2 above 92% mean spacer salbutamol and reassess; unable to talk or SpO2 below 92% means severe, so add ipratropium and steroids.

stem: 6-month-old infant presents with a history of recurrent cough and upper respiratory tract infections (URTI) about 7–8 episodes over the past year. What should we do?
OptC: Refer to ENT for tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy
why_right: About "7-8 episodes" of cough/URTI a year is within the normal range for an infant or young child, especially with siblings or daycare exposure. Without red flags (failure to thrive, severe or unusual infections, pneumonias, chronic wet cough) no investigation or intervention is needed. The useful step is reassurance plus hand hygiene, the single most effective measure to reduce spread of respiratory viruses.
why_wrong_block:
B. Prophylactic low-dose antibiotics: URTIs are viral, so antibiotics give no benefit and promote resistance; prophylaxis has a role in selected conditions (e.g. asplenia, rheumatic fever, some recurrent UTI) but not in normal childhood colds.
C. Tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy: considered for frequent, documented recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive sleep apnea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy, not for simple colds in a 6-month-old.
key_concept:
Recurrent URTIs in young children are usually normal.
  • Several viral URTIs per year is normal in infants and toddlers, more with daycare or siblings
  • Management: reassurance, hand hygiene, avoid smoke exposure
  • Red flags for immunodeficiency or CF: failure to thrive, recurrent pneumonia, severe or unusual bacterial infections, chronic wet cough, steatorrhea
  • Red flags call for workup (immunoglobulins, sweat chloride), not antibiotics
exam_pearl: Frequent colds in a thriving infant: reassure and advise hand hygiene; recurrent pneumonias or failure to thrive: investigate.

stem: An 18-month-old child is brought by his mother to the well-baby clinic for MMR vaccination. He has an upper respiratory tract infection, fever of 38.9°C, and congested throat. On examination, the child appears slightly ill. Regarding vaccination what is the best option?
OptB: Postpone vaccination until the child recovers
OptC: Give the MMR vaccine without rubella component
OptD: The second dose should be given at 4 year
why_right: A mild acute illness such as an URTI, with or without fever, is not a contraindication to MMR or other vaccines. The child looks only "slightly ill", so he should be vaccinated on schedule; deferring creates missed opportunities and leaves him unprotected. Postponement is a precaution only for a moderate to severe illness, where an ill-looking child is the deciding factor, not the thermometer alone.
why_wrong_block:
B. Postpone vaccination until recovery: right only for a moderate or severe acute illness (child looks unwell or toxic); a mild URTI in a slightly ill child does not justify delay.
C. Give MMR without the rubella component: there is no valid reason to drop a component; the combined vaccine is given, and true contraindications (severe allergy, e.g. to neomycin or gelatin, pregnancy, significant immunosuppression) apply to the whole live vaccine.
D. The second dose should be given at 4 years: does not answer what to do today; in the Saudi schedule the 18-month visit is itself an MMR dose, with another at school entry.
key_concept:
Vaccination and intercurrent illness.
  • Mild illness with or without fever: vaccinate
  • Current antibiotics or recovering from illness: vaccinate
  • Moderate/severe acute illness: defer until better (precaution)
  • MMR true contraindications: severe allergy to a component (neomycin, gelatin), pregnancy, severe immunodeficiency
  • Saudi MMR doses: 12 months, 18 months, school entry
exam_pearl: "Slightly ill" means vaccinate; "looks ill" or toxic means postpone.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot version: child visiting to get vaccine with mild fever (maybe 37) and flu-like symptoms; options Give vaccine / postpone / give inactivated and leave live attenuated. Alhomrani note: the confirmed recall literally said '38.9 AND looks SLIGHTLY ill'. Temperature differs between recalls (37 to 38.9, but not 39); in all cases answer is the same (give vaccine), unless 39 or above, then double check. If a new recall says 'looks ill' without 'slightly', reconsider. As per Nelson & UTD: mild illness with or without fever is not a contraindication for MMR.

stem: 10y/o (I’m not sure about the age) with cystic fibrosis asking when to screen for T1DM ?
OptC: No need to screen until equal or more than 18
why_right: The diabetes screened for in cystic fibrosis is CF-related diabetes (the recall says T1DM), caused by progressive pancreatic damage. Guidelines recommend an annual oral glucose tolerance test starting by age 10, because CFRD often shows only postprandial hyperglycemia that fasting glucose misses. HbA1c is unreliable in CF.
why_wrong_block:
A. HbA1c every 6 months: HbA1c underestimates glycemia in CF (increased red cell turnover) and is not sensitive enough to screen; it is used to monitor once diabetes is diagnosed, not to screen.
B. Fasting blood glucose annually: early CFRD causes post-meal hyperglycemia with normal fasting glucose, so FBG misses many cases.
C. No need to screen until 18 or older: screening starts in childhood (by age 10) because CFRD is common in adolescents and worsens lung function and nutrition.
key_concept:
CF-related diabetes screening.
  • Test: annual 2-hour 75 g OGTT
  • Start: by age 10 in all CF patients
  • HbA1c: falsely low in CF, not for screening
  • Fasting glucose: often normal early
  • Treatment of CFRD: insulin
exam_pearl: CF patient + diabetes screening = annual OGTT from age 10; HbA1c is the classic wrong answer.

stem: infant came with 4 times watery diarrhea, no fever, systemic unremarkable Your management?
why_right: An infant with "4 times watery diarrhea", "no fever" and an unremarkable systemic exam has simple acute (usually viral) gastroenteritis with no sign of significant dehydration. The cornerstone of management is oral rehydration solution with continued breast or formula feeding, plus reassurance and return precautions. Nothing here suggests the child cannot drink or is severely dry.
why_wrong_block:
B. IV normal saline with admission is for severe dehydration (lethargy, poor perfusion), persistent vomiting with inability to take oral fluids, or failure of ORS; this infant is well.
C. Stool culture is reserved for bloody or mucoid diarrhea, high fever or toxicity, outbreaks, or immunocompromise; it does not change management of simple watery diarrhea.
D. Drugs (antidiarrheals, antiemetics, antibiotics) are not used routinely in infant watery diarrhea; antibiotics need a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial cause, and antimotility agents are unsafe in young children.
key_concept:
Acute watery diarrhea in a well infant = ORS + continue feeding + reassurance.
  • No or mild to moderate dehydration and able to drink: ORS
  • Replace ongoing losses after each stool or vomit
  • IV fluids: severe dehydration, cannot tolerate oral intake, or ORS fails
  • No routine antibiotics, antidiarrheals or antiemetics
  • Do not change or dilute milk
exam_pearl: Admission and IV fluids only enter the answer when the stem gives severe dehydration signs or inability to drink.

stem: paediatric with watery diarrhea and vomiting what investigation to do
key_concept:
Watery + vomiting = think viral; bloody/mucoid + toxic = think bacterial.
  • Viral gastroenteritis: stool antigen (ELISA) or PCR; management supportive
  • Invasive bacterial diarrhea: stool culture
  • Fecal leukocytes point to inflammatory (bacterial) diarrhea, they do not confirm viral disease
  • Enteric viruses are found in stool, not by serum culture or serology

A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Stool antigen.
exam_pearl: The word "watery" with vomiting in a child steers to viral antigen testing; blood in the stool flips it to culture.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Recall text: 'what investigation to do stool antigen another was culture' (options incomplete, no answer marked).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: infant (3M) with signs of pneumonia and in examination there was bilateral crepitations, he was dehydrated and distressed, no vital signs given
why_right: A 3-month-old with "bilateral crepitations" who is "dehydrated and distressed" needs immediate supportive stabilization first: clear the airway (nasal suction), correct dehydration, and give low-flow oxygen. In an infant this age, diffuse bilateral crackles most often reflect a viral lower respiratory infection such as bronchiolitis, where management is supportive. The lead-in asks what to do now, and airway, breathing and hydration come before investigations.
why_wrong_block: A. IV antibiotics and chest X-ray do not address the immediate problems (secretions, distress, dehydration); chest X-ray is not routine in bronchiolitis, and antibiotics are added when bacterial pneumonia is suspected (high fever, toxic look, focal consolidation) after the child is stabilized.
key_concept:
Distressed, dehydrated infant with chest infection: stabilize first (ABC).
  • Suction nasal secretions (infants are obligate nasal breathers)
  • Oxygen for distress or low saturation
  • Hydration: IV or NG if unable to feed
  • Bronchiolitis: supportive only; no steroids, no routine antibiotics or CXR
  • Inability to maintain oral intake is itself an admission criterion
exam_pearl: A sick infant with diffuse crackles: supportive care beats antibiotics unless the stem gives clear bacterial clues.

stem: Pediatric patient with recurrent UTI. Mother says she does not remember if any investigations were done. Came with dysuria, Investigations showed positive nitrate, leukocytes. What is the most indicated investigation?
why_right: The key clue is "recurrent UTI" with no record of prior imaging. Recurrent UTI raises concern for an underlying anatomical problem, especially vesicoureteral reflux or obstruction, so the child needs both a renal (and bladder) ultrasound to look at structure and hydronephrosis and a voiding cystourethrogram to detect reflux. Neither test alone answers both questions.
why_wrong_block:
A. VCUG alone shows reflux and urethral anatomy but misses hydronephrosis, renal size and structural anomalies that ultrasound detects; in recurrent UTI both are needed.
B. Renal ultrasound alone is the work-up after a first febrile UTI; with recurrent infections it cannot exclude reflux, so VCUG must be added.
D. KUB ultrasound is essentially the same structural scan as renal ultrasound and does not assess reflux, so it is incomplete for recurrent UTI.
key_concept:
Pediatric UTI imaging ladder.
  • First febrile UTI (infant): renal and bladder ultrasound
  • Abnormal ultrasound or recurrent UTI: add VCUG
  • DMSA: renal scarring, done later, not acutely
  • Do VCUG once the infection is treated
  • Risk factors: VUR, posterior urethral valves, constipation, uncircumcised male, incomplete emptying
exam_pearl: "First" UTI = ultrasound only; "recurrent" UTI = ultrasound plus VCUG.

stem: Child, I think six month, diagnosed with UTI, parent ask for further assessment, which of the following initial?
why_right: In a "six month" old with a diagnosed UTI, the lead-in asks for the "initial" further assessment. Renal and bladder ultrasound is the first imaging study: it is non-invasive, radiation-free and detects hydronephrosis, obstruction and congenital anomalies. Further tests are chosen based on the ultrasound result and whether UTIs recur.
why_wrong_block:
A. DMSA scan detects renal scarring; it is done months after the acute infection in atypical or recurrent UTI, not as the initial study.
C. CT abdomen gives radiation and adds nothing for routine pediatric UTI evaluation; it is kept for complications such as suspected abscess when ultrasound is inconclusive.
D. MCUG (VCUG) is invasive and needs catheterization; it is indicated after an abnormal ultrasound or recurrent febrile UTI, not first line.
key_concept:
Initial imaging after pediatric UTI = renal and bladder ultrasound.
  • Ultrasound: structure, hydronephrosis, obstruction
  • MCUG/VCUG: reflux; if ultrasound abnormal or UTI recurs
  • DMSA: scarring; delayed, selected cases
  • CT: not part of routine work-up in children
exam_pearl: "Initial" in a child with UTI almost always means ultrasound; MCUG is the trap.

stem: 4 years old complaining of recurrent infections ( 6 sinopulmonary and recurrent gastroenteritis and more than 4 giardiasis upon and his brother died 5 months due to sepsis upon examination all lymph nodes are not palpable Which of the following is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: all lymph nodes are not palpable
why_right: A boy with recurrent "sinopulmonary" infections, recurrent gastroenteritis and repeated "giardiasis", a "brother died" of sepsis, and non-palpable lymph nodes fits X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia. A BTK defect blocks B cell maturation, so all immunoglobulin classes are low and lymphoid tissue (nodes, tonsils) is scant. Encapsulated bacterial sinopulmonary infections and Giardia are classic, and an affected male sibling points to X-linked inheritance.
why_wrong_block:
A. Omenn syndrome is a SCID variant of early infancy with erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and eosinophilia; here the nodes are absent and the child is 4.
B. This option was not recalled; any other immunodeficiency would need features this stem lacks (eczema and low platelets for Wiskott-Aldrich, normal or high IgM for hyper-IgM, later onset for CVID).
D. SCID presents in the first months with failure to thrive and opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, candida, severe viral) and is usually fatal early without transplant; a 4-year-old with mainly bacterial and Giardia infections fits a B cell defect.
key_concept:
Humoral (B cell) defect: bacterial sinopulmonary infections + Giardia, onset after maternal IgG wanes.
  • XLA: boys, all Ig low, B cells absent, T cells normal, tiny tonsils and nodes
  • SCID: early infancy, opportunistic infections, T and B both affected
  • Omenn: SCID with erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia
  • Wiskott-Aldrich: eczema, thrombocytopenia, infections
  • Hyper-IgM: CD40L defect, IgM normal or high
  • No live vaccines in suspected primary immunodeficiency
exam_pearl: Absent lymph nodes alone do not separate XLA from SCID; the age, bacterial plus Giardia pattern and male sibling point to XLA.

stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, and otitis media. Laboratory evaluation reveals normal T-cell counts and undetectable levels of IgG, IgM, and IgA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: undetectable levels of IgG, IgM, and IgA
why_right: The decisive lab pattern is "normal T-cell counts" with "undetectable" IgG, IgM and IgA. A pure failure of antibody production with intact T cells is X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia, caused by a BTK defect that stops B cell maturation. Recurrent pneumonia and otitis media from encapsulated bacteria starting around 6 months, as maternal IgG wanes, is the classic timing.
why_wrong_block: A. SCID requires profoundly low or absent T cells (combined defect) with opportunistic infections; normal T-cell counts exclude it.
key_concept:
Read the T cells first.
  • All Ig low + T cells normal + B cells absent: XLA
  • T cells low + Ig low: SCID
  • IgM normal/high, IgG and IgA low: hyper-IgM (CD40L)
  • Onset around 6 months: maternal IgG protection fades
exam_pearl: Normal T cells rule out SCID no matter how sick or young the infant is.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: version within the 659 block, printed at the top of the next page.

stem: A pediatric patient in the PICU on mechanical ventilation due to sepsis-related respiratory failure. What can we do regarding mechanical ventilation to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury?
OptA: Zero positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to prevent barotrauma
OptB: Increase tidal volume with carbon dioxide reserve
OptD: Low tidal volume to maintain permissive hypercapnia
why_right: Lung-protective ventilation is the strategy to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury in a ventilated septic child with respiratory failure. Using low tidal volumes limits alveolar overdistension (volutrauma), and the resulting rise in CO2 is accepted as long as pH remains tolerable (permissive hypercapnia). This is the same principle that reduces mortality in adult ARDS, where tidal volume is set to about 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight.
why_wrong_block:
A. Zero PEEP lets alveoli collapse and reopen with each breath (atelectrauma) and worsens hypoxemia; removing PEEP does not prevent lung injury, and adequate PEEP is part of lung-protective ventilation.
B. Increasing tidal volume causes overdistension and volutrauma, the main mechanism of ventilator-induced lung injury.
C. Hyperventilation to wash out CO2 needs higher volumes or rates, increasing lung stress, and the hypocapnia causes alkalosis and cerebral vasoconstriction; it is not a protective strategy.
key_concept:
Lung-protective ventilation = low tidal volume + adequate PEEP + limited plateau pressure.
  • Volutrauma: high tidal volume
  • Barotrauma: high airway pressure
  • Atelectrauma: cyclic collapse with zero or low PEEP
  • Biotrauma: inflammatory mediators from injured lung
  • Accept higher CO2 (permissive hypercapnia) to keep volumes low
exam_pearl: "Washing out CO2" sounds safe but is the opposite of lung protection; tolerate the CO2, protect the alveoli.

stem: A child presents with periorbital eye swelling, hematuria, and hypertension 3 weeks after impetigo. ASO positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: periorbital eye swelling, hematuria, and hypertension
why_right: "Periorbital swelling, hematuria and hypertension" is a nephritic syndrome, and it follows a "sore throat 3 weeks ago" with a "positive ASO titre". This latent period of 1 to 3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis is classic for poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome in adults (heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia), not post-infectious nephritic hematuria with hypertension.
B. IgA nephropathy gives hematuria within a few days of (or during) an upper respiratory infection; it would be right with a 1 to 2 day latency, not 3 weeks with a positive ASO.
key_concept:
Timing after infection separates the two classic causes.
  • PSGN: 1 to 3 weeks after throat (longer after skin) infection; positive ASO; low C3, normal C4
  • IgA nephropathy: hematuria within days of URTI; normal complement
