  • Membranous: nephrotic, adults, anti-PLA2R
exam_pearl: Days after the sore throat = IgA nephropathy; weeks after = PSGN.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0477).

stem: An 8 year old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother. She is concerned of bed wetting overnight despite toilet training and compared to his sister when she was in his age with good control. Which of the following pelvic muscles is affected and possible target therapy?
why_right: An "8 year old" with nighttime bed wetting "despite toilet training" has primary nocturnal enuresis. One recognized mechanism is detrusor overactivity with reduced functional bladder capacity, and the detrusor is the muscle targeted by anticholinergic therapy (e.g. oxybutynin). The lead-in asks for the affected pelvic muscle and therapy target, which points to the detrusor.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rectus abdominis is an abdominal wall muscle with no role in bladder storage or voiding.
C. Perianal muscles (external anal sphincter) relate to fecal continence and encopresis, not nocturnal bladder control.
D. Pelvic floor dysfunction is linked to dysfunctional voiding with daytime symptoms; the classic muscle target in enuresis is the detrusor.
key_concept:
Enuresis mechanisms: nocturnal polyuria (low ADH), detrusor overactivity or small bladder capacity, impaired arousal from sleep.
  • Always do a urinalysis first
  • Primary (never dry) vs secondary (relapse after being dry): ask about stressors, UTI, diabetes
  • Treatment: behavioral measures and enuresis alarm, desmopressin for polyuria, anticholinergics for detrusor overactivity
  • Recurrent UTI: renal ultrasound + VCUG; spinal signs: MRI spine
  • Age cut off for diagnosis: 5 years in DSM-5/ICCS (some sources accept wetting as normal up to 6)
exam_pearl: Asked for a "muscle" in bed wetting: detrusor; asked for first line therapy: alarm or desmopressin.

stem: A 9-month-old infant has never received any vaccinations. What should be given at this visit?
OptD: BCG, Hep B, OPV-1, Dtap-1, Measles
why_right: A "9-month-old" who has "never received any vaccinations" needs catch-up immunization: give every vaccine he is eligible for at the same visit, starting with the missed earliest doses. That means the birth vaccines (BCG, Hep B), the first doses of the infant series (DTaP-1, polio) and the age-due measles dose. Option D is the most complete listed set.
why_wrong_block:
A. BCG and Hep B alone cover only the birth doses and miss DTaP, polio and the measles dose he is old enough for; delaying them wastes a vaccination opportunity.
B. This leaves out DTaP and polio, the core primary series; giving PCV while omitting DTaP and polio does not prioritize the essential missed vaccines.
C. This is close to the routine 9-month visit for a fully vaccinated child (measles + MCV4) plus DTaP and OPV, but it omits BCG and Hep B, which an unvaccinated child still needs.
key_concept:
Catch-up rule: never restart a series, give all due vaccines at one visit, then follow minimum intervals.
  • Saudi birth: BCG, Hep B
  • 2 and 4 months: IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV, rotavirus
  • 6 months: OPV, IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV
  • 9 months: measles + MCV4
  • 12 months: OPV, MMR, PCV, MCV4
  • Rotavirus is not started late in catch-up
exam_pearl: "Never vaccinated" means catch-up from birth doses plus whatever is due now, not just the vaccines of the current age.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): Mother brought her 9-month child to well baby clinic, no previous vaccine; mother was vaccine-hesitant, then convinced: 'just give my child the necessary vaccination'. Options: A. DTaP, BCG / B. DTaP, BCG, IPV, OPV / C. DTaP, measles, BCG, Hep B, OPV (highlighted) / D. DTaP, measles, MCV 4, OPV.

stem: A full-term neonate boy presented with spontaneous soft tissue bleeding and joint swelling suggestive of hemarthrosis. Laboratory investigations showed a normal platelet count and a normal prothrombin time (PT), but the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) was prolonged. A mixing study was performed, and the aPTT failed to correct after mixing with normal plasma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
OptD: Maternal autoantibodies lead to acquired hemophilia
highlight_terms_source: aPTT failed to correct after mixing
why_right: A boy with hemarthrosis, normal platelets and PT, and an isolated prolonged aPTT points to the intrinsic pathway (VIII, IX, XI, XII). The decisive clue is that the aPTT failed to correct after mixing with normal plasma, which means an inhibitor (antibody) is present, not a factor deficiency. In a newborn, the source of such an inhibitor is maternal IgG anti factor VIII autoantibody crossing the placenta, causing a transient acquired hemophilia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Factor VIII deficiency also gives an isolated prolonged aPTT with hemarthrosis, but normal plasma supplies the missing factor, so the aPTT corrects on mixing. Right when the mixing study corrects.
B. Bernard Soulier syndrome is a platelet adhesion defect (GpIb) with large platelets, often low counts and mucocutaneous bleeding; PT and aPTT are normal and joint bleeds are not typical.
C. Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia causes petechiae and intracranial bleeding with a LOW platelet count; coagulation times are normal. Here platelets are normal.
key_concept:
Isolated prolonged aPTT: mixing study separates deficiency from inhibitor.
  • Corrects on mixing: factor deficiency (VIII, IX, XI, XII)
  • Fails to correct: inhibitor (factor VIII antibody, lupus anticoagulant)
  • Neonate with inhibitor: think maternal autoantibody crossing the placenta
  • Isolated PT: factor VII; both PT and aPTT: common pathway, vitamin K, liver
  • Low platelets + normal clotting: ITP, NAIT
exam_pearl: Same labs, but the aPTT corrects on mixing: the answer becomes factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A).

stem: A 4-week-old infant presents with projectile, non-bilious vomiting that frequently contains clotted milk. After vomiting, the child still seems to be hungry. Which of the following is the appropriate diagnostic test?
why_right: A 4 week old with projectile, non bilious vomiting who is still hungry afterwards is classic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Abdominal ultrasound is the first and diagnostic investigation: it shows a thickened, elongated pyloric muscle, is noninvasive and involves no radiation. Whether the lead in says initial, next or most appropriate, the answer for suspected pyloric stenosis is ultrasound.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal X ray may show a single bubble (distended stomach) but cannot measure the pylorus or confirm the diagnosis; it is not the test of choice.
B. Upper endoscopy is invasive, needs anesthesia and is not used to diagnose pyloric stenosis; it is for mucosal disease such as esophagitis or ulcers.
key_concept:
Pyloric stenosis: projectile non bilious vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks, hungry after vomiting.
  • Exam: olive shaped mass in RUQ / epigastrium, visible peristalsis
  • Labs: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Diagnosis: abdominal ultrasound
  • Bilious vomiting instead: upper GI contrast study (malrotation)
  • Treatment: correct fluids and electrolytes first, then pyloromyotomy
exam_pearl: Bilious vomiting flips the answer to an upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation with volvulus.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant (Q:): child with non-bilious vomiting, hungry after vomiting, visible peristalsis; most appropriate investigation: stool culture / abdominal X-ray / upper GI endoscopy / Abdominal Ultrasound (highlighted). Screenshot: 1-month-old, palpable 'olive' in RUQ, initial imaging: CT / MRI / Upper GI series / **D. Ultrasound abdomen. Note: Abdominal Ultrasound (next or most appropriate, all are same for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis). If there is BILIOUS vomiting: Upper GI contrast study.

stem: A child with liver cirrhosis due to autoimmune hepatitis, what food should he avoid?
why_right: This recall's key is fat because, in chronic liver disease, reduced bile salt secretion impairs fat digestion and absorption, so a high fat intake worsens steatorrhea and malabsorption symptoms. The recall rule is: liver cirrhosis or autoimmune hepatitis without encephalopathy, limit fat. Protein is not restricted in this setting because the child needs it for growth and to prevent muscle wasting.
why_wrong_block:
A. Protein is needed for growth in a child with cirrhosis; restriction was older teaching reserved for hepatic encephalopathy, which is not described here.
B. Carbohydrates are the main energy source and are encouraged to meet the high calorie needs of cirrhosis; they are not avoided.
D. Minerals and vitamins (especially fat soluble A, D, E, K) are supplemented in chronic liver disease, not avoided.
key_concept:
Nutrition in pediatric chronic liver disease: high calorie, adequate protein, supplement vitamins.
  • Fat: reduced bile flow causes malabsorption and steatorrhea (keyed answer)
  • Protein: maintain; old teaching restricted only with encephalopathy
  • Carbohydrate: main calorie source
  • Fat soluble vitamins A, D, E, K: supplement
  • Ascites: salt restriction
exam_pearl: If the stem adds hepatic encephalopathy, older exam recalls switch the answer to protein.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Hepatitis/liver cirrhosis/autoimmune hepatitis without encephalopathy = fat (compiler's note).

stem: Long term management of X-linked Severe combined immunodeficiency?
why_right: X linked SCID (common gamma chain defect) leaves the child without functioning T cells, and B cells do not work properly either. The only curative, long term treatment is hematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplant, ideally early in infancy before serious infections; gene therapy is an emerging alternative in specialised centres.
why_wrong_block: B. Monthly immunoglobulin replacement only covers the antibody defect and is a supportive bridge until transplant; it does not restore T cell immunity. It is the long term treatment for pure antibody defects such as X linked agammaglobulinemia.
key_concept:
SCID: absent T cell function; fatal in infancy without transplant.
  • Definitive: hematopoietic stem cell transplant
  • Bridge: IVIG, PJP prophylaxis, antimicrobial prophylaxis
  • Avoid live vaccines (BCG, rotavirus)
  • Use irradiated, CMV negative blood products
  • X linked agammaglobulinemia: lifelong IVIG instead
exam_pearl: Pure B cell defect (X linked agammaglobulinemia) flips the answer to lifelong immunoglobulin replacement.

stem: A child presents with symptoms of celiac disease and has positive anti-tTG IgA and positive anti-endomysial antibody (EMA). Which of the following is considered the definitive diagnostic test?
why_right: Positive anti tTG IgA and anti endomysial antibody make celiac disease very likely, but serology is the initial screening step. The lead in asks for the definitive diagnostic test, which is upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes. The child must remain on gluten until the biopsy to avoid a false negative result.
why_wrong_block:
A. Positive serology alone is not the definitive test here; no stem detail (such as very high tTG levels confirmed on a second sample) supports skipping the biopsy.
C. HLA DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value and is used to rule celiac disease OUT in unclear cases; a positive result does not confirm it.
D. Repeating serology in 6 months delays diagnosis; repeat serology is used to monitor adherence once the child is on a gluten free diet.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: serology screens, duodenal biopsy confirms.
  • Initial: IgA anti tTG (with total IgA level)
  • Confirm: endoscopy with duodenal biopsy
  • Keep eating gluten before testing
  • HLA DQ2/DQ8: rule out, not rule in
  • Follow up adherence: tTG levels
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten free diet
exam_pearl: Pediatric guidelines allow a no biopsy diagnosis when tTG IgA is at least 10 times the upper limit and EMA is positive on a second sample; a stem giving those details could make no further testing correct.

stem: A baby with hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia was diagnosed with congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21 hydroxylase deficiency. What is the most appropriate next step ?
OptB: IV hydrocortisone and isotonic normal saline
highlight_terms_source: congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21 hydroxylase deficiency
why_right: Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia in a baby with 21 hydroxylase deficiency is a salt wasting adrenal crisis: cortisol and aldosterone are both lacking. The immediate step is IV stress dose hydrocortisone with an isotonic normal saline bolus to restore volume and sodium; hydrocortisone also lowers potassium and raises glucose. IV dextrose is added for the hypoglycemia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone is the long term maintenance regimen once the baby is stable; it is too slow and unreliable in an acute crisis.
C. Sodium bicarbonate and insulin only shift potassium temporarily, do not treat the cortisol and aldosterone deficiency, and insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia.
key_concept:
Salt wasting CAH crisis: hydrocortisone + saline bolus + dextrose if hypoglycemic.
  • Typical age: 1 to 3 weeks with vomiting, dehydration
  • Labs: low Na, high K, low glucose, acidosis, high 17 OHP
  • Acute: IV hydrocortisone, 0.9% saline, IV dextrose
  • Maintenance: oral hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone (+ salt in infants)
  • Inheritance: autosomal recessive
exam_pearl: Stable child or asking about long term therapy: the answer becomes oral hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): child with 21-hydroxylase CAH (diagnosis was written) with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis; initial management: A. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone / B. IV fluids and IV hydrocortisone (highlighted).

stem: A 6 years old boy came to the clinic with ecchymosis post viral URTI two weeks ago. He has no hepatosplenomegaly. Labs showed low platelets. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: ecchymosis post viral URTI two weeks ago
why_right: Bruising 2 weeks after a viral URTI in a well child with no hepatosplenomegaly and low platelets is classic immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). Once the CBC shows isolated thrombocytopenia, the peripheral blood film confirms it: large platelets with otherwise normal red and white cells, excluding platelet clumping, blasts and red cell fragmentation. ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion that rests on CBC plus film.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulation profile is normal in ITP, so it does not confirm the diagnosis; it helps when a clotting disorder or DIC is suspected.
B. Bone marrow aspirate is reserved for atypical features (another cytopenia, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain, blasts) or failure to respond to treatment, where leukemia or aplasia must be excluded.
key_concept:
Pediatric ITP: isolated thrombocytopenia after a viral illness in a well child.
  • Initial: CBC
  • Confirm / next after CBC: peripheral blood film
  • Two or more cell lines low, organomegaly, bone pain: bone marrow aspirate
  • Marrow in ITP: increased megakaryocytes
  • Treat if significant bleeding: steroids or IVIG
exam_pearl: Add anemia, high WBC, bone pain or hepatosplenomegaly and the answer becomes bone marrow aspirate to exclude leukemia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Isolated thrombocytopenia (ITP): Initial, Next, CONFIRM: CBC (if present), Blood film (if CBC already done or not present). 2 cell line defect (thrombocytopenia + anemia or neutropenia): Initial/Next (without the word 'confirm'): CBC > Blood film (debated approach); CONFIRM (e.g. initial to confirm or next to confirm): Bone marrow.

stem: 6 Y/O boy brought by his mother C/o fatigue and O/E hepatosplenomegaly labs showed WBC 2.5 Hb 8 also plt low what is the next step to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: A 6 year old with fatigue, hepatosplenomegaly and low WBC, Hb and platelets has pancytopenia with organomegaly, which points to marrow infiltration such as leukemia. The lead in is confirm the diagnosis, and only bone marrow examination (aspirate and biopsy) establishes it and classifies the disease.
why_wrong_block: B. Blood film: a quick supportive step that may show blasts, but it cannot confirm or classify leukemia and may be blast free (aleukemic); it would be the answer if the question asked for the initial test.
key_concept:
Two or more cell lines down = bone marrow.
  • Pancytopenia + hepatosplenomegaly or lymph nodes: think leukemia, confirm by bone marrow
  • Pancytopenia without organomegaly: think aplastic anemia, also bone marrow
  • Isolated low platelets after viral illness: ITP, marrow not needed (increased megakaryocytes if done)
exam_pearl: Initial test = CBC and film; confirmatory test = bone marrow examination.
compiler_note:

stem: A term baby, born to a diabetic mother with respiratory distress and desatting. He is macrosomic. What is the next appropriate step?
OptA: Admit to NICU and monitor glucose
why_right: A macrosomic term infant of a diabetic mother with respiratory distress and desaturation is at risk of several problems at once: RDS (hyperinsulinemia delays surfactant), transient tachypnea, polycythemia, cardiomyopathy and especially hypoglycemia. The appropriate next step is NICU admission for oxygen support, close monitoring and serial glucose checks, escalating only if the baby deteriorates.
why_wrong_block:
B. Intubation and mechanical ventilation are for respiratory failure (apnea, severe distress or hypoxia despite oxygen or CPAP); the stem gives no such severity.
C. Immediate surfactant is not given before RDS is established and the baby is assessed; it is typically given via an endotracheal tube to a baby with confirmed RDS needing support.
D. Empirical antibiotics are right when there are sepsis risk factors (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, GBS); none are given here, and the stem's emphasis is the diabetic mother.
key_concept:
Infant of diabetic mother in distress: stabilise airway and breathing in NICU and check glucose early.
  • Hypoglycemia from fetal hyperinsulinemia
  • RDS even at term (surfactant delay), TTN
  • Polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia, hypocalcemia
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
  • Macrosomia: shoulder dystocia, Erb palsy
exam_pearl: If the stem shows apnea or severe hypoxia despite oxygen, the answer moves to airway support and ventilation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant (Q:): newborn of diabetic mother, respiratory distress and desaturation shortly after birth, macrosomia (Examiner 1: just desatting, no numbers; Examiner 2: sat in 80s); B. NICU admission, glucose monitoring, and observation highlighted. Another variant: post-term/full-term macrosomic baby of DM/GDM mother with MAS, respiratory distress and de-sating, no numbers: 1. Intubation and ventilation / 2. NICU admission and glucose monitoring / 3. wait and reassess (unmarked).

stem: A 2-month-old premature infant born at 28 weeks gestation required CPAP and supplemental oxygen for 2 months. When transitioned to nasal cannula, the infant develops a monophasic expiratory wheeze. What is the most likely diagnosis?
OptB: Tracheomalacia due to prolonged airway support/intubation
why_right: A 28 week preterm infant who needed CPAP for 2 months and now has a monophasic expiratory wheeze has acquired tracheomalacia: prolonged positive pressure and intubation damage the immature tracheal cartilage, so the trachea collapses during expiration. A single pitched (monophasic) wheeze comes from one large central airway, unlike the diffuse polyphonic wheeze of small airway disease. Diagnosis is by bronchoscopy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is chronic lung disease of prematurity (oxygen need at 36 weeks corrected age) with tachypnea, retractions and diffuse polyphonic wheeze; it does not explain a fixed monophasic central wheeze.
C. Congenital subglottic stenosis is present from birth and causes biphasic or inspiratory stridor and recurrent croup; an ACQUIRED stenosis after intubation is possible but still gives stridor, not expiratory wheeze.
D. Laryngomalacia causes INSPIRATORY stridor from early weeks, worse supine and better prone; it is not related to ventilation and does not cause expiratory wheeze.
key_concept:
Noisy breathing in infants: phase and pitch localize the lesion.
  • Inspiratory stridor: laryngeal (laryngomalacia)
  • Biphasic stridor: subglottic or tracheal fixed narrowing
  • Monophasic expiratory wheeze: intrathoracic large airway (tracheomalacia)
  • Polyphonic wheeze: small airways (BPD, bronchiolitis, asthma)
  • Tracheomalacia: bronchoscopy; laryngomalacia: laryngoscopy
exam_pearl: Inspiratory stridor worse supine since early infancy, with no ventilation history: the answer becomes laryngomalacia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same question shown twice. Numbered 707: infant born at 28 weeks on BIPAP for 2 months, off bipap developed monophasic wheeze; only A. Laryngomalacia / B. Tracheomalacia due to prolonged intubation (highlighted). Fuller 'Q:' version used here, also highlighting tracheomalacia.

stem: A child complaining of constipations. On examination there was decreased anal sphincter tone and dilated rectum with fecal impaction. Family was asking how to prevent this from reoccurrence:
why_right: Reduced anal tone with a dilated rectum and fecal impaction describes chronic functional constipation with retention: the stretched rectum loses sensation and tone. This recall's key for preventing recurrence is good toilet habits: behavioral retraining with scheduled sitting after meals, a proper footrest and positive reinforcement, so the rectum is emptied regularly and can regain size and sensation.
why_wrong_block:
B. A high fiber diet is general advice, but extra fiber beyond normal age intake has little proven benefit and can increase bulk in an already overstretched rectum; it is not the key preventive step.
C. Long term laxatives (maintenance osmotic laxative such as PEG) are used after disimpaction to keep stools soft, but they are combined with, not a substitute for, toilet training in this recall.
key_concept:
Functional constipation with impaction: disimpact, maintain, retrain.
  • Disimpaction: oral PEG (or enemas)
  • Maintenance: osmotic laxative for months, wean slowly
  • Behavior: scheduled toileting after meals, diary, rewards
  • Diet: normal fiber and fluids
  • Hirschsprung contrast: empty rectum, tight sphincter, explosive stool on DRE
  • Lax anus with neuro signs: look for spinal cause
exam_pearl: If the question asks about the step right after disimpaction or drug therapy, the answer becomes a maintenance osmotic laxative.

stem: A child previously diagnosed with HSP presents with new-onset abdominal pain, bilateral ankle swelling, and hematuria with proteinuria on urinalysis. There is also a family history of SLE. What is the most likely cause of his current presentation?
OptA: Early nephritis due to systemic lupus erythematosus
OptC: Expected with HSP due to systemic vasculitis
why_right: The child already has a diagnosis of HSP (IgA vasculitis), and the new picture of abdominal pain, ankle swelling and hematuria with proteinuria is three of the four classic HSP features (purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, renal involvement), all from the same small vessel vasculitis. HSP nephritis typically appears within weeks to months of the rash, so these findings are expected disease manifestations rather than a new illness. The family history of SLE is a distractor; it does not outweigh an established, fitting diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lupus nephritis needs features of SLE in the child (malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, cytopenias, positive ANA/anti-dsDNA); a family history alone is not evidence, and HSP already explains the renal findings.
B. JIA is a chronic arthritis (≥6 weeks) with morning stiffness and does not cause hematuria, proteinuria or abdominal pain; the ankle swelling here is the HSP arthritis/edema.
D. UTI gives dysuria, fever and pyuria; significant proteinuria with hematuria points to a glomerular process, not infection.
key_concept:
HSP = palpable purpura (legs/buttocks, normal platelets) + arthritis/arthralgia + abdominal pain + renal involvement.
  • Renal: hematuria ± proteinuria; the main determinant of long term prognosis
  • Follow-up: serial urinalysis and BP for months after the episode
  • GI complication to watch: intussusception (usually ileo-ileal)
  • Lupus nephritis: needs systemic SLE features and serology
exam_pearl: A known HSP child with new renal findings has HSP nephritis until proven otherwise; a family history of SLE is a red herring.

stem: A 2-year-old girl with fever and dysuria; treated for urinary tract infection 6 months ago. How to reduce risk of recurrent UTIs?
why_right: In a toddler with a recurrent UTI ("treated 6 months ago"), the most effective modifiable factor is bladder and bowel dysfunction: constipation compresses the bladder, causes incomplete emptying and urinary stasis. Treating and preventing constipation and establishing regular toilet habits (timed voiding, complete emptying) is the first line preventive measure and is favoured over hygiene advice alone or routine antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fruit juice (including cranberry) has weak evidence for preventing UTI in children and is not a recommended preventive strategy.
B. Long-term prophylaxis is not routine after one febrile UTI; it is reserved for selected children (e.g. high-grade VUR, frequent recurrences) given resistance and side effects.
C. Front to back perianal hygiene is reasonable advice, but when toilet training and constipation prevention is offered, it addresses the stronger risk factor (bladder and bowel dysfunction).
key_concept:
Recurrent pediatric UTI: fix the reversible risk factors first.
  • Constipation and incomplete bladder emptying: treat and prevent
  • Regular, timed voiding once toilet trained
  • Hygiene: front to back wiping in girls
  • Look for anatomy (VUR, posterior urethral valves) with imaging per guideline
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: selected cases only
exam_pearl: When "constipation" appears among UTI prevention options, it wins over hygiene and over routine prophylaxis.

stem: A 2-year-old girl with fever and dysuria; treated for urinary tract infection 6 months ago. How to reduce risk of recurrent UTIs?
why_right: Same stem as the version with a constipation option, but here that option is absent. Among the remaining choices, proper perianal cleaning and hygiene (front to back wiping in a 2-year-old girl) is the simple, non-harmful preventive measure that reduces fecal flora reaching the short female urethra. It is the best available answer for preventing recurrence after a single prior UTI.
why_wrong_block:
A. Increasing fruit juice (cranberry) has no solid evidence of preventing UTI in young children and is not recommended.
B. Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis is not routine after one UTI 6 months ago; it is kept for selected high-risk children (e.g. high-grade VUR or frequent recurrences) because of resistance and adverse effects.
key_concept:
Preventing recurrent UTI in young girls: simple measures before antibiotics.
  • If offered: treat/prevent constipation and toilet habits (best)
  • Otherwise: perianal hygiene, front to back wiping
  • Adequate fluids, avoid holding urine
  • Prophylaxis: selected cases only
exam_pearl: Check the option list: if "toilet training and preventing constipation" is present, that is the key; without it, hygiene is chosen.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same stem as 734 but without the toilet-training option; here C is highlighted.

stem: child with a history of egg allergy is scheduled to receive the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine and the influenza vaccine. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine and the influenza vaccine
why_right: Egg allergy is not a contraindication to either vaccine. MMR is grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture and contains negligible egg protein, so it is given routinely even to egg allergic children. Current guidance also allows inactivated influenza vaccine in egg allergic children, with the usual post-vaccination observation; so the child receives both. (A repeated version keys this as "give both and observe".)
why_wrong_block:
B. Withholding influenza vaccine for egg allergy is outdated; egg allergy (even beyond hives) does not contraindicate inactivated influenza vaccine.
C. Withholding MMR is wrong: egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR. MMR is withheld for anaphylaxis to gelatin or neomycin, pregnancy or significant immunosuppression.
D. Deferring both leaves the child unprotected for no valid reason; the true absolute contraindication is anaphylaxis to a previous dose or to a vaccine component.
key_concept:
Egg allergy and vaccines:
  • MMR: give (chick fibroblast culture, not egg)
  • Inactivated influenza: give, with routine observation
  • Yellow fever: contains egg protein, needs allergist assessment
  • MMR/varicella true issue: gelatin or neomycin anaphylaxis
  • Absolute contraindication to any vaccine: anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component
exam_pearl: The only egg-related vaccine to stop and refer for is yellow fever; MMR and flu go ahead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Repeated (Q:) version with options reordered: A) Give MMR but not influenza, B) Give both and observe [highlighted], C) Give influenza but not MMR, D) Do not give either vaccine.

stem: Newborn of diabetic mother with jittery movements. What to check for?
why_right: An infant of a diabetic mother has fetal hyperinsulinism from chronic exposure to maternal hyperglycemia; after cord clamping the glucose supply stops but insulin stays high, causing neonatal hypoglycemia in the first hours of life. Jitteriness is a common presenting sign, and hypoglycemia is the most frequent and most dangerous (brain injury) cause, so blood glucose is checked first.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sodium disturbance is not a characteristic metabolic problem of infants of diabetic mothers and is an uncommon cause of jitteriness.
B. Hypocalcemia does occur in infants of diabetic mothers and can cause jitteriness, but it is less common and usually later than hypoglycemia; check calcium if glucose is normal.
C. Hypomagnesemia also occurs (and accompanies hypocalcemia), but it is a secondary consideration after glucose and calcium.
key_concept:
Infant of diabetic mother: problems to anticipate.
  • Hypoglycemia (most common, first hours): check glucose first
  • Hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia
  • Polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia
  • Macrosomia, birth trauma, RDS
  • Congenital anomalies (cardiac, caudal regression)
exam_pearl: Jittery newborn of any kind: bedside glucose first; then calcium and magnesium.

stem: 4 month old infant previously had kernicterus with neurological sequelae. What is the expected finding in examination?
why_right: Kernicterus is deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia (globus pallidus) and brainstem nuclei. Basal ganglia damage produces dyskinetic (athetoid) cerebral palsy with involuntary writhing movements and dystonia, so the neurological sequelae expected on motor examination are dyskinetic.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spastic CP is from upper motor neuron damage (periventricular white matter or cortex), classically with prematurity or HIE, not bilirubin injury of the basal ganglia.
C. Hypotonia can be seen early in bilirubin encephalopathy, but it is nonspecific and evolves; the characteristic chronic sequela is dyskinetic movement.
D. Ataxic CP results from cerebellar damage, not basal ganglia injury.
key_concept:
CP type by lesion site:
  • Spastic: pyramidal tract/white matter (prematurity, PVL)
  • Dyskinetic/athetoid: basal ganglia (kernicterus, HIE)
  • Ataxic: cerebellum
  • Chronic kernicterus tetrad: athetosis, upward gaze palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, dental enamel dysplasia
exam_pearl: Kernicterus to basal ganglia to dyskinetic (athetoid) CP; do not be pulled by "spastic", the most common CP overall.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): A baby (No Age) with kernicterus and has neurological sequelae. What you will expect on his motor examination? A. Spasticity, B. Ataxia, C. Hypotonia, D. Dyskinesia [highlighted].

stem: A child with symptoms suggestive of functional constipation. Which of the following supports the diagnosis?
OptB: Sacral dimple and loss of anal tone
OptC: Normal intake and two stools per day
why_right: Functional constipation in children is defined clinically by infrequent (≤2 per week), hard or painful stools with withholding, large stools and fecal incontinence (soiling) from overflow around a retained mass. "Infrequent hard stool with soiling" combines these core features and supports a functional diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. A sacral dimple with loss of anal tone is a red flag for spinal dysraphism or tethered cord (organic, neurogenic bowel), arguing against functional constipation and needing spinal imaging.
C. Normal intake with two stools a day is a normal bowel pattern and does not support constipation at all.
key_concept:
Pediatric functional constipation (clinical diagnosis, no tests needed):
  • ≤2 stools per week, hard or painful stools
  • Withholding behaviour, large diameter stools
  • Fecal incontinence/soiling (overflow)
  • Red flags for organic cause: delayed meconium, failure to thrive, abnormal spine or anal tone, ribbon stools, bilious vomiting
exam_pearl: Soiling in a constipated child is overflow, a feature of functional constipation, not a sign of diarrhea.

stem: A child presents with a 4-day history of dark urine and jaundice that was preceded by diarrhea. Some children in his school have similar symptoms. Lab tests show elevated liver enzymes. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: 4-day history of dark urine and jaundice
Some children in his school have similar symptoms
why_right: Jaundice and dark urine with raised liver enzymes, preceded by GI symptoms, in a child with similar cases at school is an outbreak of acute hepatitis A (fecal-oral spread). Hepatitis A in children is self-limiting with no specific antiviral, so management is supportive: hydration and rest, with monitoring for liver failure.
why_wrong_block:
B. Acyclovir treats herpes simplex/varicella infections; HSV hepatitis is a concern in neonates or the immunocompromised, not a school outbreak of jaundice.
C. Antibiotics have no role in viral hepatitis; they would fit bacterial infections such as ascending cholangitis or bacterial dysentery.
key_concept:
Hepatitis A:
  • Fecal-oral, outbreaks in schools/daycare
  • Prodrome (GI upset, fever) then jaundice, dark urine
  • Diagnosis: anti-HAV IgM
  • Treatment: supportive; no chronic carrier state
  • Monitor PT/INR and mental status for acute liver failure
  • Contacts: vaccine or immunoglobulin post-exposure
exam_pearl: School or daycare cluster plus jaundice = hepatitis A = supportive care.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Numbered 744. A fuller 'Q:' variant with different distractors (liver transplant, Rabivirne) is carded separately.

stem: A four-year-old child presented to the pediatric ER with a four-day history of dark urine and jaundice preceded by diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. She’s attending a daycare school where multiple episodes with kids have been reported. ALT was 600. AST was 500 high. What is the most indicated management?
highlight_terms_source: four-day history of dark urine and jaundice preceded by diarrhea
daycare school where multiple episodes with kids have been reported
why_right: A 4-year-old in daycare with multiple similar cases, with GI prodrome followed by dark urine and jaundice and transaminases in the hundreds (ALT 600, AST 500), has acute hepatitis A. It is self-limiting in children, so the indicated management is rest and hydration with monitoring (PT/INR, mental status) for the rare progression to liver failure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver transplant is for acute liver failure (encephalopathy, severe coagulopathy); a well child with raised enzymes alone does not meet that threshold.
C. Acyclovir is for herpes virus infections (e.g. neonatal or immunocompromised HSV hepatitis), not a daycare hepatitis A outbreak.
D. Ribavirin ("Rabivirne") has no role in hepatitis A; there is no specific antiviral therapy for HAV.
key_concept:
Acute viral hepatitis A in children:
  • Clues: daycare/school cluster, GI prodrome, jaundice, dark urine
  • Confirm: anti-HAV IgM
  • Manage: supportive (rest, fluids, avoid hepatotoxic drugs)
  • Prognosis marker: PT/INR
  • Transplant only for acute liver failure
exam_pearl: High transaminases alone do not mean liver failure; INR and encephalopathy decide escalation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 744; different option set, same concept (hepatitis A outbreak, supportive care).

stem: A 7-month-old infant is brought to clinic with a 2-day history of vomiting and diarrhea. The stool is watery without mucous or blood. examination reveals that the infant is only mildly dehydrated. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This is acute watery gastroenteritis ("without mucus or blood", likely viral) with only mild dehydration. Management is oral rehydration (ORS) with continued feeding and reassurance, since the illness is self-limiting; no antibiotics or anti-emetics are needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cefixime is unnecessary: antibiotics are for bacterial infection (e.g. bloody diarrhea with systemic features), not watery diarrhea with mild dehydration.
C. Anti-emetics are not routine; a single dose of ondansetron is kept for persistent vomiting that prevents oral rehydration, which is not described in this mildly dehydrated infant.
D. Both parts are unnecessary: no indication for anti-emetics, and cotrimoxazole is not indicated without confirmed bacterial infection.
key_concept:
Gastroenteritis by dehydration level:
  • Mild to moderate: ORS (with continued feeding)
  • Severe, failed ORS or cannot tolerate oral: IV fluids
  • Antibiotics: confirmed/suspected bacterial cause (bloody stool, systemic toxicity)
  • Avoid routine anti-emetics and anti-diarrheals in infants
exam_pearl: Watery, bloodless, mildly dehydrated infant: ORS and reassurance; adding drugs is the trap.

stem: A 4-year-old child with biliary atresia underwent a Kasai procedure. Postoperatively, he develops pruritus with excoriations and has elevated serum bile acids (120 µmol/L). What is the most appropriate treatment for his pruritus?
why_right: After a Kasai procedure, bile flow is often incomplete, so bile acids build up and cause cholestatic pruritus ("pruritus with excoriations", "elevated serum bile acids"). Cholestyramine is a bile acid binding resin that traps bile acids in the gut and interrupts their enterohepatic circulation, lowering the pruritogenic load. It is the classic first-line symptomatic treatment for cholestatic itch in children.
why_wrong_block:
B. Diphenhydramine only sedates; cholestatic itch is not histamine driven, so antihistamines do not treat the cause. It may be used as a night-time adjunct, not as the main treatment.
C. IV corticosteroids do not relieve established cholestatic itch and add infection risk; steroids are sometimes given early after a Kasai to promote bile flow, which is a different goal from treating pruritus.
D. Vitamin K corrects coagulopathy from fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption in cholestasis; it does nothing for itch. It is right when the question shows a prolonged PT/INR or bleeding.
key_concept:
Cholestatic pruritus = retained bile acids; treat by removing or diverting them.
  • First line: bile acid sequestrant (cholestyramine)
  • Other options: ursodeoxycholic acid, rifampicin
  • Cholestasis also needs fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) supplementation
  • Persistent failure of the Kasai: liver transplantation
exam_pearl: Itch in cholestasis is bile acid driven, not histamine driven: pick the bile acid binder, not the antihistamine.

stem: 1 years old presented with lower weakness, noted by the mother. The abdominal and pelvic CT showed mass coming from the paravertebral sympathetic chain. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest cells of the adrenal medulla and the paravertebral sympathetic chain, which is exactly the origin described on CT. Paraspinal tumours can grow through the neural foramina (dumbbell lesion) and compress the spinal cord, explaining the "lower limb weakness" in a 1-year-old. Young age, extra-renal origin and neurological signs all point to neuroblastoma.
why_wrong_block:
B. Wilms tumour arises from the kidney itself, distorting the collecting system; it is usually a well child with a flank mass, hypertension or hematuria, not a paravertebral mass with cord compression.
C. Retinoblastoma is an eye tumour presenting with leukocoria or strabismus; it does not produce an abdominal paravertebral mass.
D. Hepatoblastoma arises in the liver (right upper quadrant mass, raised AFP) in infants and toddlers; it does not come from the sympathetic chain.
key_concept:
Neuroblastoma vs Wilms tumour:
  • Origin: adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain vs kidney
  • Midline: may cross vs usually does not
  • Mass: fixed vs mobile
  • Constitutional symptoms: common vs uncommon (child well)
  • Associations: opsoclonus-myoclonus vs WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann
  • Neuroblastoma: paraspinal spread can compress the cord
exam_pearl: "Sympathetic chain" or "adrenal" in the stem = neuroblastoma; "arising from the kidney" = Wilms.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 'Child with abdominal mass passing or related to spinal cord' (options Neuroblastoma / Williams / Hepatoblastoma), Neuroblastoma highlighted.

stem: A 6-year-old child with asthma is now complaining of cough, increased asthma attacks, and more frequent use of his inhaler. The mother reports that the father smokes one pack per day inside the house, and the mother uses shisha on weekends. What should be done to prevent worsening of the child’s symptoms?
OptB: Tell the mother to stop using shisha or reduce it
OptC: Advise the parents to reduce the child’s exposure to smoking
highlight_terms_source: father smokes one pack per day inside the house
why_right: The child's worsening (more cough, more attacks, more inhaler use) has an obvious trigger in the history: the father smokes "inside the house" and the mother uses shisha. The question asks how to prevent worsening, so the priority is trigger avoidance: counsel both parents to remove the child's exposure to all tobacco smoke. Option C is the only one that covers both cigarettes and shisha and addresses the cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stepping up corticosteroids treats poor control but leaves the trigger in place; environmental triggers, adherence and technique are addressed before escalating therapy.
B. Only addresses the mother's weekend shisha and ignores the father's daily cigarette smoking indoors, the larger exposure; it is a partial answer.
D. A face mask does not reliably protect a child from indoor smoke and is not a recommended prevention strategy; the exposure itself must be removed.
key_concept:
Worsening asthma: check triggers, adherence and inhaler technique before stepping up.
  • Tobacco smoke (cigarettes, shisha) is a major modifiable trigger
  • Best counselling: smoke-free home and car, offer cessation support
  • Step up therapy only after these are addressed
exam_pearl: When the stem hands you a trigger (smoking at home), the answer is removing the trigger, not more medication.

stem: A boy with a known history of asthma (not sure if this) presents to the clinic with cough and shortness of breath. His father reports that he “never smokes in the same room as the child,” and therefore believes his smoking has no effect on the boy’s health (something like that). What is the most appropriate counseling for this parent’s?
OptA: Advise him not to smoke at the same room with the child for their safety
OptB: Advise Him To Smoke Outside Of The House And [KEEP ON SMOKING HABIT] (Eee Wallah It Was Written Like This)
OptC: Explain The Risk Of Second Hand Smoking That Linger His Child & Increase Asthma Risk (I Don’t Remember What It Is , I Just Remember The Word “Linger” & Second Hand Smoking)
highlight_terms_source: never smokes in the same room as the child
why_right: The father believes that "never smoking in the same room" protects his son. Tobacco smoke spreads through the home and its residues linger on clothes, hair, furniture and surfaces (third-hand smoke), so the child is still exposed and his asthma risk rises. The most appropriate counselling corrects this false belief by explaining the risk of second-hand and lingering smoke, which opens the door to quitting.
why_wrong_block:
A. This restates what the father already does; smoking in another room does not prevent exposure, so it reinforces his misconception instead of correcting it.
B. Smoking outside reduces but does not eliminate exposure (residue on clothes and hands), and endorsing continued smoking misses the chance to counsel cessation.
key_concept:
Parental smoking counselling in an asthmatic child:
  • Second-hand smoke: inhaled directly from the environment
  • Third-hand smoke: residue lingering on clothes, skin and surfaces
  • Separate rooms or ventilation do not make a home smoke-free
  • Goal: explain the risk, then advise and support cessation
exam_pearl: "I don't smoke in the same room" is a misconception to correct, not a safe practice to endorse.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer line reads 'C??' (uncertain).

stem: A colic baby with leg raise and crying ( there was no swaddling or white noise )
why_right: Crying episodes with leg raising in an otherwise well infant describe infantile colic, a benign, self-limited condition that usually settles by around 3 to 4 months. Management is supportive: reassure the parents and teach soothing strategies. With swaddling and white noise not offered, reassurance is the remaining correct supportive option.
why_wrong_block: B. Herbal teas have no proven benefit for colic and may displace milk feeds in a young infant; they are not recommended.
key_concept:
Infantile colic (rule of 3s): crying more than 3 hours/day, more than 3 days/week, for more than 3 weeks in a healthy infant.
  • Typical in the first 3 months of life
  • Management: reassurance plus behavioural soothing (holding, rocking, swaddling, white noise)
  • No medication or routine formula change
  • Red flags (fever, vomiting, poor weight gain, blood in stool) need workup
exam_pearl: Well, thriving infant with paroxysmal crying and drawn-up legs = colic: reassure, do not medicate.

stem: Mother of a 2-month-old infant complains that her baby has frequent episodes of excessive crying for 3 hours, raises legs and passes gas. What is the appropriate management?
OptB: Swaddling and use of white noise
why_right: A 2-month-old with excessive crying for "3 hours", leg raising and gas, with no red flags, has infantile colic. Treatment is reassurance and behavioural soothing, and swaddling with white noise is a recommended soothing technique. It is the only option that is safe and recommended for this benign, self-limited condition.
why_wrong_block:
A. Simethicone has no proven benefit over placebo for colic, despite the "passes gas" clue; medication is not recommended.
C. There is no fever or sign of infection; antibiotics have no role in colic.
D. Imaging is for red flags such as bilious vomiting, a mass, fever or poor growth (for example intussusception); a well infant with typical colic needs no investigation.
key_concept:
Colic = diagnosis of a well, thriving infant; management is non-pharmacological.
  • Rule of 3s: more than 3 h/day, more than 3 days/week, more than 3 weeks
  • Peaks in the first 3 months
  • Soothing: holding, rocking, swaddling, white noise, parental support
  • Avoid: simethicone, colic drops, routine formula change
  • Episodic crying with vomiting, lethargy or mass in an older infant = think intussusception
exam_pearl: "Passes gas" tempts you to simethicone; colic is treated with soothing and reassurance, not drops.

stem: 6 years old boy came to clinic with , pale and Ecchymosis and petechiae post upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago ،boy now is well demarcated of bruising and petechiae . ( lab platelets was low cant remember the exact number) what is most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis. Low Platelets Normal Hb Normal WBC
highlight_terms_source: post upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago
Low Platelets Normal Hb Normal WBC
why_right: Petechiae and bruising 2 weeks after a URTI in a well 6-year-old with isolated thrombocytopenia (normal Hb, normal WBC) is acute childhood ITP. ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the peripheral blood smear confirms it by showing true thrombocytopenia (excluding clumping) with large platelets and no blasts, schistocytes or other abnormal cells. A typical picture plus a normal smear is enough to make the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulation factors (PT, aPTT) are normal in ITP; they are right when bleeding suggests a factor problem such as hemophilia (joint or deep bleeding, prolonged aPTT) or DIC.
B. Bone marrow examination is reserved for atypical features, such as abnormal Hb or WBC, blasts, organomegaly, bone pain or failure to respond, where leukemia or marrow failure must be excluded.
D. Antiplatelet antibody testing has poor sensitivity and specificity and is not used to diagnose ITP.
key_concept:
Childhood ITP: isolated low platelets after a viral illness in a well child.
  • Typical age 2 to 6 years, usually acute and self-limited
  • Confirm: CBC plus peripheral smear (large platelets, otherwise normal)
  • Marrow if done: normal or increased megakaryocytes
  • Bone marrow only if atypical (cytopenias in other lines, organomegaly, bone pain)
  • Management: observation if only skin bleeding; IVIG or steroids if severe; platelets only for life-threatening bleeding
exam_pearl: Low platelets with normal Hb and WBC = smear; add anemia, high WBC or bone pain = bone marrow for leukemia.

stem: Child with high fever sore throat and mild erythematous rash O/E multiple mosquito bites, how to manage: Vitals are stable except for fever of 39
highlight_terms_source: high fever sore throat and mild erythematous rash
why_right: High fever, myalgia, a mild erythematous rash, multiple mosquito bites and borderline platelets suggest a viral infection, most likely dengue in a mosquito-endemic setting. With "stable vitals" and no warning signs, management is supportive: oral hydration and paracetamol for fever, with monitoring for warning signs. Fluids are the cornerstone because plasma leakage is the main danger.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs are avoided in suspected dengue because they worsen bleeding risk with falling platelets; paracetamol is the antipyretic of choice.
B. The picture is viral and the child is stable; empiric antibiotics are indicated only for suspected bacterial sepsis or an unstable, toxic child.
key_concept:
Suspected dengue (fever, myalgia, rash, mosquito exposure, low or falling platelets):
  • No warning signs: oral fluids, paracetamol, rest, close follow-up
  • Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin (bleeding risk)
  • Warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, rising hematocrit with falling platelets: admit for IV fluids
  • No role for antibiotics or steroids
exam_pearl: Fever with mosquito bites and low platelets: paracetamol plus fluids, never ibuprofen.

stem: Which of the following viral gastroenteritis can be prevented by vaccination?
why_right: Rotavirus is the only listed cause of viral gastroenteritis with a licensed vaccine. It is an oral live attenuated vaccine given in infancy and is part of the Saudi routine schedule starting at 2 months, which has greatly reduced severe dehydrating diarrhea in young children.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adenovirus (enteric types) causes childhood gastroenteritis, but there is no licensed vaccine for adenoviral gastroenteritis.
B. Astrovirus causes mild gastroenteritis in young children; no vaccine is licensed.
C. Norovirus is the leading cause of outbreak gastroenteritis across all ages, but no vaccine is licensed yet.
key_concept:
Viral gastroenteritis causes and prevention:
  • Rotavirus: severe watery diarrhea in infants; oral vaccine in the routine schedule from 2 months
  • Norovirus: outbreaks (cruise ships, schools), all ages; hygiene only
  • Adenovirus and astrovirus: milder pediatric disease; no vaccine
  • Diagnosis when needed: stool antigen (ELISA)
exam_pearl: Only rotavirus gastroenteritis is vaccine preventable; norovirus is the common distractor.

stem: 7 year old boy his father has TB , he has PPD of 14 mm , CXR is negative , what is the next step?
why_right: The child is a household contact ("father has TB"), a group in which a TST of 5 mm or more is already positive, so 14 mm is clearly positive. With a negative CXR (and no stated symptoms) active disease is excluded, which makes this latent TB infection. The next step is to treat it (chemoprophylaxis, for example isoniazid or a rifampicin based regimen) to prevent progression to active TB.
why_wrong_block: B. IGRA is an alternative screening test (useful when BCG makes a TST hard to interpret), not a confirmatory step after a clearly positive TST in a close contact; repeating testing only delays treatment.
key_concept:
Positive TST + normal CXR + no symptoms = latent TB: treat it.
  • ≥5 mm positive: recent contact of active TB, HIV, immunosuppressed, fibrotic CXR
  • ≥10 mm positive: children under 4, high risk settings, migrants from endemic areas
  • ≥15 mm positive: no risk factors
  • Abnormal CXR or symptoms: work up for active TB (sputum or gastric aspirate) and give full therapy instead
  • LTBI options: isoniazid 6 months, rifampicin 4 months, or isoniazid + rifampicin 3 months
exam_pearl: Cutoff depends on risk group: a contact with ≥5 mm is positive; an abnormal CXR switches you from prophylaxis to active TB workup.

stem: 11 yo female with signs and symptoms of SLE and anti-dsna positive With low complements She is on mtx already What to add
why_right: Hydroxychloroquine is the cornerstone of therapy for every SLE patient unless contraindicated, and it reduces flares and organ damage. This child has active serology (anti-dsDNA positive, low complements) and is on methotrexate alone, with no renal or CNS disease described, so the missing backbone drug is hydroxychloroquine (HCQ + MTX is the standard mild to moderate combination).
why_wrong_block:
A. Cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe organ threatening lupus, classically neuropsychiatric lupus or severe nephritis; no such involvement is described.
C. MMF is the preferred immunosuppressant for lupus nephritis; it would be right if proteinuria, active sediment or rising creatinine were given, not as the next add on here.
key_concept:
All SLE gets hydroxychloroquine; then match the add on to the organ.
  • Skin and joints: HCQ + methotrexate (± low dose steroid)
  • Kidney (lupus nephritis): MMF
  • CNS (neuropsychiatric lupus): cyclophosphamide
  • Life threatening disease: high dose steroid + immunosuppressant
  • Pregnancy: stop MMF, switch to azathioprine, continue HCQ
exam_pearl: If the patient is not on HCQ yet, adding HCQ beats escalating to a stronger immunosuppressant unless kidney or CNS involvement is stated.

stem: Patient 11 y with every symptom of active SLE malar rash and active arthritis but no cns on renal problems 100% sure the labs all are the classic labs ex c3 was low and creatinine normal but the patient is not on any drug and they did not say he was diagnosed before What is the management now?
why_right: This is a new, untreated SLE ("not on any drug") with skin and joint disease (malar rash, active arthritis) and no renal or CNS involvement (normal creatinine). That is mild to moderate lupus, and hydroxychloroquine is the cornerstone first line drug for every SLE patient; low C3 reflects activity but does not by itself demand cytotoxic therapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Azathioprine is a steroid sparing or maintenance agent (and the pregnancy compatible substitute for MMF), not the first drug in new mucocutaneous and joint lupus.
C. Cyclophosphamide is for severe organ threatening disease, classically neuropsychiatric lupus; the stem explicitly says no CNS involvement.
D. MMF is the choice for lupus nephritis; it would fit if proteinuria or active urinary sediment were present, but renal function is normal here.
key_concept:
New SLE without kidney or CNS involvement: start hydroxychloroquine.
  • Mild to moderate (skin, joints): HCQ, then add methotrexate and low dose steroid if not controlled
  • Nephritis: MMF
  • Neuropsychiatric lupus: cyclophosphamide
  • Anti-dsDNA and low complement track activity, especially renal
exam_pearl: "No CNS, no renal" is the clue that removes cyclophosphamide and MMF; HCQ is the default.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Answer: B' printed at top of next page.

stem: 4 years old with night time enuresis , never been dry , his mother is worried , what is the most reasonable advice you can give? (Written like this)
OptD: I don’t recall but something wrong
why_right: Night time wetting in a 4 year old who has never been dry is primary nocturnal enuresis, and bladder control at night is not expected until about age 5. With no daytime symptoms, red flags or other complaints described, the most reasonable advice is reassurance that this is within normal development and usually resolves spontaneously (a urinalysis is a reasonable simple check).
why_wrong_block:
A. Urology referral is for red flags: daytime symptoms with recurrent UTI (renal US and VCUG), abnormal neurologic or spine findings, or a structural cause; none are described.
B. Behavioral therapy (alarm, reward charts) is used for persistent enuresis after about 5 to 6 years; at 4 years it is premature and can add stress.
D. This option was not recalled; whatever it was, active intervention or referral is not needed for monosymptomatic enuresis at this age.
key_concept:
Enuresis is diagnosed only from about age 5; below that, reassure.
  • Primary: never dry; secondary: wet again after a dry period (look for stress, UTI, diabetes)
  • Every child: urinalysis
  • Recurrent UTI: renal US + VCUG
  • Spine deformity or abnormal neuro exam: MRI spine
  • Persistent after 5 to 6 years: enuresis alarm first, desmopressin as alternative
exam_pearl: Age decides it: a 4 year old wetting at night is normal; a previously dry child who starts wetting is secondary and needs a cause.

stem: Preterm presents with nasal flaring and grunting. What is the appropriate management?
OptD: Insert 2 tubes in the bronchus (something similar)
why_right: A preterm infant with grunting and nasal flaring has respiratory distress syndrome until proven otherwise, caused by surfactant deficiency of the immature lung. The definitive treatment is exogenous surfactant given intratracheally (with respiratory support such as CPAP), which improves compliance and reduces mortality and air leak.
why_wrong_block:
B. Corticosteroids prevent RDS when given to the mother before preterm delivery; they are not the treatment for an infant already showing RDS.
C. Antibiotics are added when sepsis or congenital pneumonia is suspected (maternal fever, PROM, chorioamnionitis); they do not treat surfactant deficiency, which is the problem in an otherwise unremarkable preterm.
D. Chest tubes or bronchial intubation are for complications such as pneumothorax or for ventilation, not the specific management of RDS.
key_concept:
Preterm + grunting, flaring, retractions = RDS: CPAP and intratracheal surfactant.
  • RDS: preterm, ground glass CXR with air bronchograms
  • TTN: term, often C section, fluid in the fissure, resolves in 1 to 3 days
  • Meconium aspiration: post term, meconium stained liquor, patchy infiltrates
  • Prevention: antenatal steroids to the mother in threatened preterm labor
  • Maternal diabetes delays surfactant maturity, so RDS can occur nearer term
exam_pearl: Steroids prevent RDS (mother, before delivery); surfactant treats it (baby, after delivery).

stem: One new question about 6 month child came with his father to clinic c/o reducible pulge in center of his abdomen increase with crying
highlight_terms_source: reducible pulge in center of his abdomen
why_right: A reducible bulge at the center of the abdomen (umbilicus) that increases with crying in a well 6 month old is a classic umbilical hernia: a fascial defect through which skin covered contents protrude with raised intra-abdominal pressure. Most close spontaneously, so the usual plan is observation.
why_wrong_block: B. Omphalocele is a congenital midline defect present at birth, with bowel or liver covered by a membrane (amnion and peritoneum) and the cord inserting into the sac; it does not appear later as a skin covered bulge only on crying.
key_concept:
Skin covered, reducible umbilical bulge on crying = umbilical hernia: observe.
  • Most close spontaneously by about 2 to 4 years
  • Surgery: incarceration or strangulation, or persistence at about 4 years
  • Strapping or coins do not help
  • Omphalocele: membrane covered, at birth, associated anomalies
  • Gastroschisis: right of the cord, no sac, exposed bowel
exam_pearl: Skin covered and appearing later = hernia; membrane covered and present at birth = omphalocele.

stem: Child glucose 38 Blood sample taken before correction not mention about mother hx Insulin fasting 40 was normal regarding refrence range was upto 110 ACTH 500 was slightly high What is the cause of
why_right: The key is the critical sample taken during hypoglycemia (glucose 38, "before correction"). During true hypoglycemia insulin should be fully suppressed, so an insulin value that is merely "normal" is inappropriately high and points to hyperinsulinism. The mildly raised ACTH fits the expected stress response to hypoglycemia rather than primary adrenal failure.
why_wrong_block: A. Adrenal insufficiency causes hypoglycemia with low cortisol and a suppressed insulin; it would be the answer if cortisol were low with a clearly high ACTH (often with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or hypotension), not with unsuppressed insulin.
key_concept:
Interpret every hormone against the glucose at that moment.
  • Hypoglycemia + detectable or "normal" insulin = hyperinsulinism
  • Hyperinsulinism also shows low ketones and low free fatty acids
  • Low cortisol + high ACTH = primary adrenal insufficiency
  • High ketones with appropriately suppressed insulin: ketotic hypoglycemia, hormone deficiency
  • Always draw the critical sample before giving glucose
exam_pearl: A "normal" insulin during hypoglycemia is abnormal; normal ranges apply only to normal glucose.

stem: 6 years old Patient with clear case of brucellosis. Hx of Drink raw milk patint had pain in the knee. Which if the following is the first line treatment ?
why_right: Brucellosis (raw milk, joint pain) in a 6 year old: the adult first line regimen is doxycycline based, but tetracyclines are avoided in children under 8 years because of tooth staining and bone effects. The pediatric first line is therefore TMP-SMX plus rifampicin for 6 weeks; a combination is needed because monotherapy relapses.
why_wrong_block:
B. Doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks is first line for adults and children 8 years or older; at 6 years doxycycline is avoided.
C. Ciprofloxacin alone is monotherapy (high relapse rate) and quinolones are not first line in brucellosis, especially in children.
D. Ceftriaxone has poor intracellular activity against Brucella and is not a standard regimen; single agent therapy also relapses.
key_concept:
Brucellosis always needs combination therapy; age and pregnancy pick the partner.
  • Adults and children ≥8 years: doxycycline 6 weeks + rifampicin 6 weeks (or streptomycin for the first 2 to 3 weeks)
  • Children under 8: TMP-SMX + rifampicin for 6 weeks
  • Pregnancy: rifampicin based, avoid doxycycline
  • Spondylitis or sacroiliitis: about 12 weeks
  • Neurobrucellosis: about 6 months
exam_pearl: Same disease, different answer: the child's age under 8 removes doxycycline.

stem: Name of the reflex? (images: infant held upright with feet touching surface, making stepping movements)
why_right: The images show the infant held upright with the feet touching a surface, making alternating step movements. This walking-like response is the stepping reflex, present at birth and normally fading in the first couple of months.
why_wrong_block: A. Rooting reflex: a mouth response, turning toward a touch on the cheek or corner of the mouth; it involves no leg movement.
key_concept:
Name the reflex from the stimulus:
  • Feet on surface, upright: stepping
  • Dorsum of foot touches table edge: placing
  • Cheek stroked: rooting
  • Head turned supine, fencing posture: ATNR
  • Head drop: Moro
  • Held face down toward table, arms extend: parachute (appears 8 to 10 months)
exam_pearl: Sole touching the surface gives stepping; the top of the foot touching an edge gives placing.
